COUNTY BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON.- WAR IN SOUTH AFRICA. OUR VOLUNTEERS AND THEIR WELCOME HOME. The Committee appointed at the Public Meeting held on Tuesday. the 6th instant, to carry out the arrangements for affording our local Volunteers a hearty welcome, and for pommerrating their valour and loyalty to the Queen, have decided, by the kind permission of the Rector, to hold a Thanksgiving Service in the Parish Churth, to be followed by a Public Dinner in the Parr Hall and a Smoking Concert in the evening. The Committee have also decided to place noon permanent record the names of the Volunteers. including Yeomen and Members of the Ambulance Brigade, but whether the Tablet for such purpose shall take the form of a Bronze Plate to be erected in the Town Hall, or a Public Memorial to be erected upon a site to be selected in the Town, cannot very well be decided until it is ascertained what funds are available for the purpose. The Committee are also of opinion that Presentation Swords should be given to Captain Appleton and Lieutenant Carey, and also to Captain Crolfv.ld and Captain Ridgway, each of whom holds a Commission in our Volunteer Battalion. It has also been decided to present each Volunteer with a Framed Illuminated Commemoration Card, which will contain a suitable record of the men's services. The suggestion that each man should be presented with a silver medal has had to be abandoned for the reason that the War Office would not consent to the men wearing such a medal when in uniform. The proposal that a Memorial should be erected in the Parish Church in commemoration of those who have died in South Africa will depend upon the funds available for the purpose.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

tIY DrAR NELLIE, One of the most remarkable novelties among the hats prepared for this season is the flat-crowned tcque that has its rather broad brim curved upwards at the sides and back. This 'headgear is oftenest seen in grey, white, or cream felt, the under-side of the brim being lined, as it weie, with narrow flat bands of deeper-hued velvet, while folds of silk or small rosettes surround the crown, a single upstanding aigrette being placed at the back, rather towards one side. This type of hat, however, is not universally becoming, and it is not likely to be generally popular. The toques of less conspicuous eccentricity are broad and wide in shape and are made of cloth, panne, or velvet, usually o some rather bright hue, with a touch of white introduced by means of a big rosette or a fan-bow of glace silk. A deep blue velvet toque, for instance, had its folds lined with a much paler shade of the same, while at the side, under the slightly-raised brim, was a rosette of white glace with a paste buckle in the centre.

Fashion gives you every encouragement to make your own muffs. The latest arc constructed of tulle puffed up into little billows all over, and trimmed with a spray of flowers, rich autumn chrysanthemums for choice in the front. It is perishable and sounds a cold muff, but with a lining of thick wadding and silk it is cosy enough. Much thicker gloves are worn now; the antelope ones are particularly comfortable, and so are the so-called winter suedes. Russet tints are very seasonable, even the roses in the autumn toques are tinted to assume the red-browns of the time of falling leaf and fading flowers, and seem likely to be popular.

A very pretty evening dress was ..lade of yellow brocade over tucked yellow satin. The bolero and overskirt are bordered with jewelled passementerie, and the lace bertha is edged with dark fur. A few folds of creamy chiffon are laid beneath the dress round the shoulders with a very soft becom- ing effect. The sleeves are in the now fashionable shape once sailed "marquise," and all the newest evening gowns have those elbow sleeves. These are made of lace, and are trimmed with bands of jewelled embroidery, and bordered with creamy chiffon. Many of the chiffon evening blouses are a mass of tuckings and gaugings. The quantity of work makes them expensive. Others are made with lace or embroidered boleros over colour.

The fashionable lace tie is one of thase that fold three times round the neck, falling in ends without any loops or bows. The hat which was worn with this is black chiffon with folds of white laid over it, and a long feather at the side. Some even- ing cloaks are made of pink, blue, or creamy chiffon arranged in little frills, the high collar covered with frills and lined with lace. Others have frills of lace covering them, an ermine collar sometimes consorting agreeably enough with the lace and chiffon. A lovely pink evening cape is in tucked glace with a deep fall of creamy lace headed with a narrow band of skunk. The collar is skunk, and the fronts of the cape are bordered with similar fur. At either side of the fur collar is a cascade of lace which, when the cape is fastened, forms a rippling fall ot creamy softness below the chin. The fur collar is lined with ruched chiffon very closely gauged. Fastening the bodice and skirt together is apt to throw too much weight on the shoulders, whereas when the bodice is detached from the skirt the weight is distributed more evenly. There is no necessity that the belt should be any tighter than the band of a dress made in the'housemaid style, provided that the bodice and skirt are both well. cut and fit properly about the waist. Many people nowadays wear bodices cut on the blouse system, very slightly boned and with a thin lining, shaped to the figure, but not quite tight-fitting. The skirt is sewn to a band and worn over the bodice without another belt. If you prefer your skirt sewn to the bodice there is no reason why you should not have a gown made in this way, as if you arrange the skirt to fasten over at the side and have a deep corselet belt of silk or satin, care. fully cut and boned (it need not be tight), to wear over the join, it will be impossible to tell that the dress is not made in the more usual way. Some fashionable skirts fasten down the front, and you could have yours so arranged if you preferred it. Your loving JENNIZ

During the past week or two public attt rrioa has been directed in a very marked way to two of the thrones of Europe. There is the illness of the Cz is of Russia, which everyone will rejoice to hear is taking' a favourable course, and there was the alarming incident in Germany when a mad woman hurlel an axe at the Kaiser, happily without doing any damage. When the two Emperors succeeded to the thrones of Germany and Russia it was feared that their unacquaintance witn the horrors of war, would make them less relucsant to enter upon strife than their fathers, who bad witnessed all:the terrible suffering and consequences of war. But happily these apprehensions have proved groundless, and in fact the illness of the Czsr has served to remind the people of Europe how much the peace of the world may depend upon hislilajesty's life, which everyone in this country will hope to see long preserved, if only because ef the near relationships existing tetween the Russian, as well as the German royal families, and our own. Tha repeated attacks upon Royal and distinguished personages have made the Insurance Companies very reluctant to take the risk of Anarchist outrages. It is well known that the lives of many Sovereigns, and members of the Royal Families of Europe are heavily insured,and more than one Company which was involved in considerable losses by the assassination of the late Empress of Austria, and the late King Humbert of Italy, has decided to issue no free policies to royalties. No doubt they have also been influenced in this decision by the attacks upon the Prince of Wales, and the Shah of Persia, and the fact that the treatment of Sipido, by the Belgian authoritiee, has been in every way unfortunate, and rather calculated to encourage Anarchist activity than otherwise.

The marriage of the Duke of Manchester to MISS Zimmerman was not unexpected in Society circles, but until after the event, few were aware that the wedding bad quietly taken place in London, in the presence of a few friends. The bride. who is twenty-one, is the daughter of Mr. Eugene Zimmerman, an American rail- way millionaire, who is said to have regarded her attachment to the Duke—who has followed the varied career of a journalist, and ac or, and who financial positioniis not a very satisfactory one—with considerable disfavour. The Duchess, however, decided to take her destiny into her own hands, and it is to be hoped th at she will not lose her father's good wishes, in entering the privileged circles of the British peerage. As is the case in the Marlborough family, it is not the first time that a Duke of Manchester has crossed the Atlantic for a bride. Consuelo Yznago, who married the eight Duke, and is the mother of the present Duke of Manchester, is a Spanish-American woman. There are now in fact three Dowager Duchesses of Manchester, namely, Lady Blackwood, who married the sixth Duke, the present Duchess of Devonshire, who married the seventh Duke, and Consuelo Yznago, who is the widow of the eight, and mother of the present (ninth) Duke, who it will be remembered lost, not long since his only sister—one of the loveliest girls society hes ever seen— Lady Alice Montagu. The announcement that Parliament will assemble on the 3rd of December, has caused consieerable satir- faction among London tradesfolk,who will, undoubtedly reap much benefit from tee arrangement. The men will come to town to legislate, the women to shop. and until Christmas is with us, and gone, the hotels, fashionable restaurants, theatres and other places of amusement, promise to be crowded. All things point to the season of 1901 being a particularly brilliant one, and already modistes are busy with sketches and ideas for gowns for the February Drawing Rooms. There will be an unusual number of debutantes, so many who were to have been presented this year having wisely waited for brighter times. Princess Alice of Albany, who will be eighteen in February will be the cnly Royal debutante. According to a well-known, and wealthy society woman, who hails from across the "pond "it is a much more costly affair to bring out a girl in America, than it is in this country, her elaborate wardrobeess debutante, often exceeding that of many brides. In the case of her two daughters she estimates that from their first outfit, to that provided for them at eighteen, when entering society, the sum expended on each was over £12,000! This includes, she goes on to say, education and travell- ing expenses, also jewellery, How many otherwise well-dressed girls are but in differently shod! For this there is now no excuse, as Anyone who visited the shoe and leather fair, at the Agricultural Hall, London, mu-t admit. Of course if a good article is desired, a good price must be paid, but many girls who cheerfully spend guineas on accessories consider a few shillings will suffice to purchase a pair of boots or shoes. This is a mistake, and should be remedied forthwith. A chat with an expert in the Hall revealed the fact that the greatest difficulty a buyer ex- periences, is, to get orders made" up to sample," a sad refisction on the integrity of the British manufacturer. However, as a set off to this—it appears that England still maintains her pre-eminence in the matter of boots and shoes, and that these are superior to the American, in excellence of style, and suitability to the tastes and habits of British wemen. AU the Same the American pattern is being copied by the Stafford houses, in cut stitching, and the numerous gradations of size, and for this latter let us be devoutly thankful. There is no doubt that the American type of footgear—being longer and narrower than our own—is far more becoming. The English type causes the foot to bulge out in a very ugly way, wbilst it cramps the toes unmercifully. The most fashioneble style at present for town wear, on fine days, is glace kid, in brown or black, with straight patent leather caps and facings. Satin shoes, matching the gowns in colour, will be worn for balls, whilst for ordinary evening wear, fine black or coloured kid, or suede, with paste buckles, or other ornaments are shown at the hest shops. A great number of 'smart evening shoes come from Vienna. They are vary well cut, and have dainty linings in delicate shades. Brown leather will be more than ever employed in the spring, but the exhibition makes it plain tbat the white shoe is a thing of the past. The appearances of the members, who attended the recent meeting of the Rational Dress League at For- cheater Hall, Bayswater, in " costume," showed that this style admits of individuality and of great variety, but that it is utterly lacking both in elegance and grace, goes without :sayiog. Viacountessl Haberton, who took the chair, might well have been mistaken for one of the opposite sex. Her dress (?) of brown-grey homespun bore a striking resemblance to a masculine shooting suit, and her closely cropped hair, and hard felt hat naturally heightened thefillusion. Her only concessions to feminine vanities was a yellow brocade vest and lace tie, and the fact that years ago men disported themselve in satins and laces was doubtless the explanation of this frivolity. That" rational ' dress makes little or no progress is evident to all One reason perhaps is that few of us are sufficiently strong-minded to bear the notoriety, and ridicule, such attire inevitably brings upon the wearer, Then again the British woman's foot and ankle, is not her most fascinating point,and she, knowing this,dreads all unnecessary exposure of the effending member. And last, but by no means leastewho among us could censent to the "'cropping" process deemed desirable by ext. me " ratienaliste.' That " rationale " are safer than saute is an indisputeble fact, but provided the latter are built with due regard for the purposes for which they are re- quired, there is really very little to shriek about. There is much needless waste in cooking potatoes, for in peeling and cutting they are often reduced to half their size. The most nourishing part of this vegetable too, is that which is just beneath the skin. It is best therefore, to thoroughly wash the potatoes, leave their " coats "on and steam until done. Lst them dry a few moments, remove the skins, place them in a vegetable dish with a little butter, pepper and salt on them. Put them in the oven to melt the butter, ar d serve. This is a far more economical, wholesome, and tasty way ef dressing potatoes than the ordinary method of peeling and boiling. " MADGE."

div.p: THE HOUSE BY THE RIVER.
Dv MRS. C. N. IVILLIAMSON,
Author of "The Secret of the Pearls," "The House by the Lock," "Queen Sweetheart," "The Barnstormers," "Her Royal Highness," Zw.
CHATTER XIII.
THE TWO MEN WHO LOOKED AT symL.

The pair lvho now entered the office were of a very different order front the man at the desk. They were both young—the elder not much over thirty, well-dressed, with an air of conscious importance and prosaerity ; they came, not from outside, but front MP inner room, which Hester, looking up a, the door opened, could see was com- fortably furnished in r: manner very superior to thia small outer office.

The two gentlemen scarcely glanced at Hester, but their eyes at once fell upon Sybil's face, which was turned towards them in profile, and continued to dwell there with a show of interest. Plain as was her dress, the simple hat spoilt by the drizzling rain of last night, it was easy to see that she was very different from the sort of girl who usually applied for a position in the Robertson Addressing Agency. A faint gleam of sunlight struggled through the dusty window-panes as if for the sole purpose of illumining the cameo-like out- line of her features, the flower texture of her skin, and_the pale gold of her rippling hair. She looked a young princess in the disguise of a Cinderella, as Hester Frayne thought, observing with vague apprehension the appreciative gaze of the two men. "Well, haven't you got your name on paper yet? Time is money here, and!if yoh write as slowly as that it would be no use your applying for a berth, even if we had a dozen open," the man at the desk said, brusquely. Hester at once guessed, from the sudden change for the worse in his manner, that one of the new- comers was his employer, before whom he wished to appear eager that not a single moment should be wasted. As Sybil allowed him almost to snatch from her hand the paper on which she had just finished writing, Hester wondered greatly what name and what address she had chosen on the spur of the moment; and she would have given a good deal to peep over Sybil's shoulder without attracting the attention of Miss Monstance, who was eyeing both the girls with disapproval ; perhaps with suspicion. But:I-rester could not contrive to satisfy herself, and had to appear solely interested in blotting her new name selected at random. She had put down the number of the house and the name of the street where she wished presently to find lodgings and hoped that Sybil might have been quick-witted enough to do the same. "Pretty enough hand for a young society lady" (he pronounced it "lydy "), commented the man at the desk, examining Sybil's specimen of penman- ship, "but not sufficiently clear and businesslike for us. I'm afraid it's no good your leaving your address. You must learn to write a different sort of hand before you apply at our establishment again." He was evidently conscious still of his employer's presence, for the two men who had come in from the next room seemed inclined to linger and listen to the conversation instead of passing through by the outer door as they had apparently intended doing at first. "Let's see the young lady's handwriting, Kittredge," said the younger of the pair, and advancing he took the paper from the desk where the manager had carelessly laid it. "I don't want to dispute your judgment," he went on, after a glance, "but it strikes me it isn't a bad thin.- to have cinnllars addressed sometimes, in sending to a certain class of persons, by a hand that looks like that of a lady, not a woman of business. Makes that sort of person readier to open the envelopes instead of chucking them into the waste-paper basket, as I'm afraid they too often do. Suppose you take the young lady on and see how she gets along. Put her on to the society work, you know." "Very well, sir," reluctantly consented Mr. Kittredge, with a glint of suppressed rage in his eye. Sybil looked gratefully up at the man who had arrived so opportunely to intercede for her. She was far from guessing that it was her beauty and grace which had won for her the opening she had been about to lose, and she put down the .piece of good luck which had suddenly befallen her entirely to the proprietor's kindliness of heart. "Thank you so much," she could not help saying, with a childlike smile of gratitude, and a bright blush which rendered her a hundred times prettier than before. "But my friend, is there a place for her, too? We are very anxious to keep together." "I daresay Mr. Kittredge can manage it if your friend's writing is legible and good,' graciously returned the proprietor, never taking his eyes from her face. "Eh, Kittredge ? " The manager sulkily criticised the slip of paper submitted to him by Hester. "Not bad," he pro- nounced. "We had several applications in answer to our advertisement some hours ago, and the young women have settled down to business. I did not expect to take on anyone else at present, but as we have rather a press of work this week, counting in the order Mr. Make has just given us "—he glanced at his proprietor's companion—"we can use a couple more assistants for a time at any rate, no doubt." _ . _

At the name of "Drake," Hester Frayne started slightly, and looked with veiled intentness at the man indicated. She had lately seen that name, figuring prominently in a memorandum written in a pocket-book she had found; and to hear it now, in the place to which she had brought Sybil Wade as a refuge from the owner of that pocket-book, was disconcerting, to say the least. She tried to think that it was only a coincidence, reminding herself that Drake was not at all an uncommon name, and that there were nine chances in ten against this friend of an agent for addressing circulars having any acquaintance with the man in her thoughts. But she was ill at ease, and the fact that "Mr. Drake" had evidently observed her start and glance with decided quickening of interest was not reassuring. If she had known the initials of the person who figured in the memorandum merely as "Drake" she could presently have satisfied her doubts ; but as it was she must only hope for the best, since it would be foolish to give up the situation just secured in cowardly terror of a chance so unlikely. "I won't say anything about it to that poor child," Hester thought. "It would only worry her for nothing, and she has enough trouble to bear as it is."

"By eTOVe ! That's a pretty girl you've got there," said the friend of the proprietor as they went out together. "A lady come down in the world. There's good birth and breeding in every feature, and the very way she has of carrying her head and shoulders. I shouldn't wonder if that girl had a history worth knowing." "If I find it out I'll let you know," returned Mr. Robertson, of the Addressing Agency, laughing. "The other girl's nothing wonderful, except that her eyes are good. Might be Beauty's maid. She seemed rather attracted by you though, I thought." "She did give a sudden look round when she heard your manager speak my name," returned Drake, drawling a little, with an affectation of indifference. "I can't flatter myself that her interest was any more personal than that. Who knows but some unfeeling namesake of mine has eiraged her young affections only to spurn them? For the girl certainly glared as if the name of Drake hadn't the pleasantest associations. By the way, while we're on the subject of names what does Beauty call herself ?" "‘ Sara Ward, 19, Thameston-street, City- road,' was what she had written in a very pretty hand on the piece of paper Kittredge had given her," said Frank Robertson, who was a distant cousin of Drake's, springing from a humbler, more m comercial branch of the family. His great ambition, now that he had made a little money, was to obtain a place in society and gain entrance Co his cousin's "set." He was always greatly flattered by a call from Beauchamp Drake, who •sometimes gave orders to the agency; and in return for such small favours as his "smart" relative deigned to bestow he was ready to lend money, or oblige in any other way. Robertson had not failed to be struck by Sybil Wade's beauty, but he would scarcely have troubled to set his manager's decision aside had Drake not whispered extravagant expressions of admiration in his ear. Now he was pleased to supply all information within his power, and, having a defective memory, had been at some pains to remember the written name and address. _
"Sara Ward," thoughtfully echoed Beauchamp Drake. "Well, I hope Sara Ward will prove her- self fit for the post she has got, as I should be sorry to hear that she'd been discharged and

Anished into space before I have a chance of. another glimpse of her. lam almost foolish in my admiration for pretty faces, you know; quit tne - artist soul, • as my mother used to say when .1. Was a youngster." "Oh, I can promise you that no such disaster as her disappearance shall happen," rejoined the other, with somewhat ponderous gaiety of manner. "I'll see to that myself. While as or the little loan we were discussing in my room, I can manage it at once."

"That's a good fellow!" exclaimed Drake. "You shall have the money again after Christmas. Hope I can do you a good turn sometimes to ma-se up for the many you constantly do for me." "As to that, you and your partner, Mr. Anson, are very kind about sending us any work you have to give out. Besides, if you—if you could—" "If I could what, my dear chap ? " "If you could contrive to include me—er—in that dinner you mentioned that you were giving next week it would be a big step for me. Earls and Viscounts are every day affairs to you, I sup- pose, Ent I don't know any, even on business; and I wouldn't mind if I could get one or two as . acquaintances. That sort of thing sounds well, and as I am working my way up I have to think of it." Beauchamp Drake laughed rather contemptuously, though he despised in his cousin an attribute largely developed himself. "The party's made up, but I'll think it over and see what I can do," he said. "I'll tell you what," and he laughed ;."we'll let it depend on one thing. You see, if you come in I shall have to ask some- body else to make the number right, so it will be rather a lot of bother, and you'll owe me some- thing in return----" ' _ _ _

"if it's about the money pay me when you like —or not at all," ejaculated Robertson. "It isn't the money. To tell you the truth I've a special reason for wanting to know that girl who calls herself Sara Ward. That sort of person holds herself stiffly sometimes, you know, and she would probably resent it very much if I tried to scrape an acquaintance with her as she went in or out of your office. You must help me, and if you play your cards so that I can have a talk with her alone without frightening or making her angry, sometime within the next few days, why, you shall come to that dinner of mine which you seem to fancy will be so desirable."

"It's as good as done!" exclaimed Robertson, enthusiastically. "But, I say, I never knew you to be bowled over so completely at first Sight of a pretty face before." • "No, you never did, nor I either," admitted Drake, with a peculiar sparkle of the eye. It was true; he had hardly exaggerated his admiration for Sybil; but her beauty alone would never have induced, him to make his present request, or his present promise. A very curious idea had crept into his mind as he stood in his cousin's office looking at the two girls who applied for situations; and, as he had acknowledged to Robertson, he had his own special reasons for wishing to follow it up.
CHAPTER XIV.
THE LETTER FOR MISS WARD.

Hester had not counted on having to begin work at, the office immediately; but this was insisted on by Mr. Kittredge, who deeply resented what he considered the slight put upon him and was determined to shew that in spits of what had occurred, his authority was not to be despised. So it was that the two strangely-assorted friends were obliged to delay securing their lodgings, though they had already written down their names as dwellers at a certain address. They were shewn into a room, adjoining the outer offices, where between twenty and thirty women, young and old, sat writing with a fierce eagerness, as if life itself depended upon the increasing number of brown wrappers, or narrow white envelopes, which they addressed and added to the growing piles before them. Directories were funkished Sybil and Hester—or rather, Miss Sara Ward and Miss Mary Carter, as their names now appeared on the list of the agency's employs. Hester had to address wrappers (in which circulars were to be enclosed) to the doctors and dentists of a certain neighbourhood in the west district of London. Sybil's work, according to Mr. Robertson's suggestion, was in a different line. She had handsome, thick white envelopes, of a better quality than those supplied to any of the.wornen whom she could see; on these it was her day to inscribe the names of various titled persons, beginning with the letter "A," and working through the alphabet, as far as she had time to go. Mr. Robertson's employes were paid by the number of addresses they were able to write during working hours, but all those envelopes which were blotted, or otherwise defective, must be discarded from the pile; and a fine was exacted for each duplicate inadvertently written or any mistake in the direction.

As short an interval as possible was taken for lunch, which was brought to the office in paper bags by most of the employes; and through hour after hour no sound was heard in the place save the scratching of many pens, the rustling of paper, or the suppressed exclamation of some unfortunate one who had found herself guilty of an error. It was six o'clock when they all stopped, and the atmosphere of the room, without a wir open, was close and almost insupportable. Sybil's head ached, and her back and limbs were cramped, as she ,passed out into freer air; but she was buoyed up by a strange feeling of excitement. If the mystery of her father's fate had not weighed heavily upon her, she could have been almost happy, despite fatigue, and the consciousness (pressed upon her by Hester) of her own continued danger. She liked to feel that she was to be in- dependent, that she would be able to support herself, and she was still warmly grateful for the kindness of Mr. Robertson in granting her such a ahance. But for him, they might have tramped wearily from place to place all day, finding no one who wanted their services; but for him, she might have had to break into poor Hester's smell funds for her expenses. She had worked at dtsperate speed, that he might know, and feel justified for his good-natured interference, and her nerves were strained to highest tension as she and Hester left the office. It was already nearly dark, and though they were hungry as well as tired, they decided to go straight to Thameston-street, near the City-road, and engage a room if one were to be had. "Wasn't it odd," said Sybil, as they hurried along through the twilight, "among the envelopes I addressed to-day was one to a cousin of my own? It seemed strange to write the name, and think how little he would guess who had written it." Hester stopped suddenly at the corner of Thameston-street. "A cousin of yours?" she sharply repeated. "Do you mind telling me the name?"

"Lord Carstairs," Sybil answered, simply. "Oh ! 7 The little word, as Hester uttered it, was a gasp rather than an exclamation, and the arm to which Sybil was clinging gave a slight nervous jerk. • Sybil was startled. "Why, what is the matter ? " she asked.

"Nothing,, nothing," Hester hastily assured her. "I had a cramp in my hand, from writing so long, I suppose. Yes, it was queer, on your very first day at your new work, to find yourself addressing a letter to one of your relations. How do you know he would not guess who had written on the envelope? Are you—sure lie had never seen your handwriting before ? " "I'M very sure. I never wrote to him or any of his people." said Sybil. "I hardly thought about their existence until—until the night before I met you. Then, you know, I was dining with my father at the house of an old friend'bf his, and Lord Carstairs, with his mother and sister, was there. I did forget a handkerchief with my name on it, which I had myself written in indelible ink; when I got home afterwards, I found that I had left it behind, and I thought I could recall laying it on a table where I had been looking over a book of engravings at Lady Northmuir's house. But it is not very likely that. Lord Carstairs saw it, or would hp,ve remembered the handwriting if he had. So he can't guess that the poor relation of the family is hiding and making herself even more despicable than before (as Lady Carstairs and Gladys would certainly think!) by addressing envelopes for a living." "You didnot like your cousins ? " Hester said, abruptly. "I admired them; they are all handsome," Sybil evasively returned. "But I suppose we don't often like people whom we think dislike us. I should have been very unhappy among them, and thankful to get away from them all at last, if—" She checked herself suddenly, for she had begun to say something on the impulse of the moment, which she would not have cared to say if she had stopped to reflect, and she was very glad that, Hester did not question her, as she had hale expected. It would have been awkward to refuse, but—she could not have mentioned Jack Churchill's name.
The elder girl was slowly walking on again now, and so far from asking Sybil to finish .the broken

sentence, she haa hardly heara it. one was very taciturn until they had reached No. 19, Thatneston-street, the house they had seen adver- tised in the paper and Sybil (who attributed her companion's sudden mood ot siienoe to fatigue or pain) would have been greatly surprised if she had guessed how Hester's thoughts were dwelling on a lost handkerchief, inscribed in indelible ink with the name of Sybil Wade. Already, in the interest of ringing the house- bell and inquiring for lodgings, she had forgotten even mentioning the loss pf her handkerchief; nor did it recur to her mind for many a day to come. No. 19, Thameston-street, was a house of grim afld. forbidding aspect. The narrow passage into which the front door opened, was covered with worn and soiled linoleum; the very walls, with their tern. dark paper, were depressing, and the slatternlY maid who answered the bell looked ready to break into tears. Mitchell-street, Bloomsbury, had been a Paradise to this; yet when they learnt from a sour-visaged landlady that all her rooms; excel:4 one on the top floor, were full, Sybil felt that she ought to be glad of a shelter even -here. "A beautiful, double bed-sitting-room," we° Mrs. Wool's description of the one vacant apart- ment ; but, having toiled up three flights of stairs to inspect it, Sybil and Hester were not surprised at her willingness to let it for what she called the "nominal sum of six shillings a week." They took the room, because they had given the house as their address to Mr. Kittredge, of the agency, and because they had not the strength or the courage to look further that night. When the matter was settled, and a week's rent paid ill advance (according to Mrs. Wool's custom, when lodgers came in without luggage). Hester bravely mentioned the two names which now appeared on the books at Rebel tson's. "Miss Ward and Miss Carter," the landladl. glibly repeated after her. "Why, that explains the mystery." "What mystery ? " Hester inquired, quickly, her suspicions ever ready to catch fire. "A letter coming here for Miss Ward-IWS Sara Ward," replied Mrs. Wool. Sybil flushed, and threw a hurried glance of astonishment at Hester. "A letter here for me '' she ejaculated. "It came here; but it isn't exactly here netA said the landlady. "If you thought of comillp and told folks to send things to this address, you a better have let us know. A messenger brought the letter, and I happened to answer the door myself. 'Does a Miss Sara Ward live here ? ' says he. 'Sot: says I, 'she doesn't. Never had a person of that- name in the house, as far as I can remember. Then the boy looked down at an envelope he taken out of his little wallet, and seemed to be undecided what to do. I advised him to leave it, as perhaps the one who'd sent the note to thi° house knew his business, and Miss Ward would be coming here sooner or later. But the felloW wouldn't do that. He'd been told she lived here, and he must take the letter back, to ask what the' gentleman wanted him to do next." "The gentleman!" exclaimed Hester. "You are sure the boy said that ? " "Sure," responded Mrs. Wool. "Were:a° expecting something important ? " She looked at Sybil, though she replied to het friend; for Sybil was "Miss Ward." "I —I don't quite know," faltered the, girl; greatly puzzled. She could hardly wait until the woman should go, and leave her two lodgers alone, to talk the strange event over with Hester. At last thel were able to speak—in low voices, to be sure, lest\ Mrs. Wool should be curiously-minded, and still lingering at the keyhole. "There is only one thing we can be certain of,. said Sybil, "the letter must have come from the agency. Yet why should anyone there wish t° write to me, especially while I was still in the office? Perhaps the manager, who seemed 15° angry at being told to keep us on, has written to discharge us, and say that we are not to come back again." Hester shook her head. "I only wish I could think it was anything as simple as that," she said,' dolefully. "I've got a horrid presentiment that something's very wrong, though I'm as much in the dark as you are. I had rather a shock in the office. I didn't mean to worry you by telling you. then, but maybe you'd better know now. That man called Drake—l didn't like his being there. Someone we have got to dread had a friend of that name, and the coincidence, frightened me—though I hope there's nothing in it. Still—l don't like that letter coming here. It seems as if eaerYadV were against us." "Do you think we ought to go away from °lle house ? " asked Sybil, desperately. She was so tired, and she could not help thinking that Hester looked on the dark side too Still, she had put herself in Hester's hands, ana felt bound to go where Hester went. "I can't make up my mind," answered the eldet girl. "If only one knew whether the letter Noel°. be sent here again. But lam afraid of messenger.. boys for you. You can guess why." touch 1 "Couldn't we go out and get something to eat ? meekly suggested poor Sybil. "If we weren, _Ar hungry and forlorn, we should be able to tau' more clearly."

Hester did not answer for a moment, but c:011" tinned to stare gloomily out through the window into darkness; and, while Sybil waited her verdict, $ quick knock came at the door. Both girls started, as they had heard no warilini sound of footsteps outside, and before they given permission to enter, Mrs. Wool threw open. the door. "That messenger's come back," she announcei3. °with the letter for Miss Ward." (To be continued.)

div.head: VISIT TO WALTON
div.p: A VISIT TO WALTON
HALL.

Although the Master of. the Belvoir is of neces- -,sty resident on the borders of Leicestershire and lencelnshire during the six months of winter and early spring, he is not in the true sene3 of the term, .80 completely "at home" there as in his native Cheshire, tor he spends as much of his time as possible daring the rest of the year ar, Walton Hall, a charming residence situated within three miles of Warrington and yet removed from the smoke and the grime of a town Which Ruskin, had he ever Paessd that way, would assuredly have condemnsd for having no artistic beauty. But Warringtote if It ails short of the ideal in this respect, is a pro - .per)ee plaeo, and one in which many greet fortunes have bdc n built up, its prosper ty being in a great Measure due to the fact that it ie not dependent Upon a single industry alone, so that if one branch of trade happens to-be depressed, the odds are that • some of the others will be doing well. But the rapid extension of the town and its suburbs does not effect the quietude and privacy of Walton Hall, 'Which is reached by a bridge over the Manchester Ship Canal, since the making of which a new road has been constructed. Once over this unlovely but no doubt useful waterway, you soon reach the park - gates, and a fine drive of nearly a mile in length, through an avenue of limes planted by Sir Gilbert's father, brings you to the front entrance of Walton Hall, which, it may be added, though having War- rington for its post town and railway station, is not in Lancashire but in Cheshire. The main entrance faces almost due north, and the house, which was built about sixty-five years ago. is of red brick, faced with stone, over which the ivy has been allowed to spread ; and from the north entrance there is a very fine view over the lawns which lead down to the new conservatories, of which Sir Gilbert Greenall is justly proud, as he drew all the plans himself and does his own land • seeping. Thus in former times the park, which is about a hundred acres in extent, came right up to the house, but he has sunk a fence and laid out gardens to the east and south which add very much to the attractiveness of the place. There is a circular walk round the garden, from one paint of which there is a good view over the Bridgwater `Canal and the Mersey Valley, an i the late Sir Gilbert Greenall was wont to say that you could See from this spot more invested capital than anywhere in the world. There is much else that is interesting to be seen outside the house, for although the hunters are all at Selvoir, Sir Gilbert ?a ,o fond of horses that the stables which, havel .been and are still being enlarged, will repay a visie.l They contain some thirty-five or forty carriagel horses and hackneys, most of them being of quitel excsptional quality. The harness-room is a paragon I of neatness an smartness, while adjacent to the' .stables is the roomy coach-house, containing a great variety of carriages for general use, among them being two of the old family chariots, which have never been out during the last thirty or forty years except- when they conveyed Sir Gilbert's two Sisters, on the occasion of their marriage, to the Parish church, which is on the borders of the park and was built by their father. It is a startling con- trast to see by the side of these two chariots— • Painted yellow like all the rest of the carriages—a motor-ear, of which, however, Sir Gilbert will die- claim the ownership, and he is net quite easy in I his mind as to whether he has done right in giv- ing shelter to it for his cousin. Close by is the large riding school, the walls of which are plastered thick .with cards .denoting the hundreds of prizes which Sir Gilbert has won at, the different shows with his horses, his 'ponies. and his pigs. He cannot, unfortunately, :show you his fine stud of ponies, descended from Mr. Christopher Wilson's famous sire. Sir George, for this is at Aehbourne, in Derbyshire, Where the land is better eui tee for hree lino. But, no one with any sense of what was right would think of leaving Walton without paying a visit to the piggeries, the inmates of which cover them-elves with glory wherever they go. Sir Gilbert. started the herd himself, and he keeps pigs of the three white breeds, and with them be !wins nearly all prizes whersver they are exhibited. People with a deli- cate olfactory sense may be inclined to take the pigs for granted ; but the buildings in which they snooze contenteely through the day are as clean as a esery, and their inmates would be ungrateful in- deed if they did not win prizes .for their master after the care that is bestowed upon them. Special crates have been made so as to convey them with the utmost comfort from their stye to the show- ground without break of d ; they are wa3he from. time to tinie,an,l.happily for them, they know nothing of the inevitable en-I. Sir Gilbert has alss a good stud of hackneys, deseended from the Oldest iorkshire blood ; but these, like the ponies tire not to be !leeii. at Walton, as they are kept, in No'rfolk. It is time, however, to say something of the interior of the house, which is a very comfortable one end contains many good pictures and much good statuary, for the late Sir Gilbert Greenall was I a warm patron of art, and did much to assist Mr. Luke Fildiss and his brother-in-law, Mr. Henry Woods, both natives of Warrington, in their early days. There are two fine pieces of sculpture in the front hall, one being Gibson'a " Minstrel Boy." In the dinine-roem,facing east, are portraits by Millais of the late Sir Gilbert Greenall and his wife, the latter presented by tenants on the estate. The por- trait, of the late Sir Gilbert is considered to be one of the best Millais ever painted, and among other pictures in this room is a head of St. Paul by I Murille, Sir Joshua Reynolds's portrait of the engraver of his picture, and one of Sidney Cooper's pt-tidies of sheep. In the drawing-room, which faces north, is the first work ever done by Warring-1 ton Wood, a young man whom the late Sir Gilbert sent out to. Rome to study under Gibson, and this is a statue of Rachel,which gave that. artist a capital -start, The library, which is on the other side of the hell, and has a fine view over the Mersey Valhi, is more lived in, and it has some very good oak panel- ; and of oak is the tandsome staircase which leads from the hall to the upper rooms, on the, walls being a portrait of a man (name unknown) who was one of those who came Alive out of the Li-bon earthquake, an address presented to Sir Gilbert upon his coming of ace, and eome Crown Derby chins. The decoration of the new ceiling is also very fine, and there is much of interest to see in the new part of the house. which was added in 1870, and contains the billiard-room: Sir Gilbert's own study, and the bou- doir of his sister, who. married to their cousin. Mr 'Cyril Greenall. had kept house for him both here end at, Wool-dhorpe, where they resided during thel 'hunting season. until Sir Gilbert married, a mouth ago, his cousin, Miss Frances Griffith, who is a !laughter of Captain Wynne Griffith, formerly let Royal Progoons, and niece of Captein Park-Yates, ep well known in the Che.hire country. In the billiard-room is a portrait of Jones,the noted hunts- man of the North Cheshire, which was in the Aca- demy, while cf more immediate intere4 to Sir Gil- bert ie a series of old Belvoir pictures and a portrait by Cathie rt Bradley of the celebrated hound Dexter who is a great grandson of the Belvoir Gambler. ji.Pre ton, is a • nhetogreph of Sir Gilbert in the bvery of the Terrorley Hunt Club, which meets for a week in the beginning of November to hunt, and to dine, but sinee he has assumed the master- hp of the Belvoir he hes been obliged to forego th.e4 pleasant fixture. His own room adjoins the lulliard-room, and here are to be seen Alken's water-eolotire, portraits of Lord Forester, Lord eombermere.the Duke of Hutland, end Lord Henry Bentinck, a " Vanity Fair" caricature of Sir Gilbert

himself, and some good pictures of prize-winning animals by Palfrey. 5 Here, too, are pictures, as children, of the late Sir Gilbert Greenall and his twin brother, the Arch- deacon of Chester, and although it is only within the last seventy years that Walton Hall has been built, the Greenalls have been resident in the neighbourhood for two or three centuries, while they were also maltsters at St. Helens, as several monuments in the parish church there tesi.ify. It way at St. Helens, too, that the great brewery which has an equally important establishment at. Wag- rington, was founded, and this was for some time held in partnership with the Lyon family, which is still represented in the district. The late. Sir Gilbert Greenall was a man of vast wealth, .which he put to the best possible use, building and endow- ing churches and schools, and doing all he could to ameliorate the condition of the poor. He was a thorough-going Conservative, and sat for War- rington in most of the Parliaments between 1847 and 1892. He lost the election of 1868 through an error in counting on the part of the Mayor's 'clerk, and this let in that sturdy Radical, ." Peter Rylauds ;" but Mr. GreenalLas he then was,regained the seat in 1874. In 1880, when the Liberal flood- tide was at is height, he was beaten by Mr. McMionies ; but he was again returned in 1885. this time, as the inscription on a large bowl (the gift of the Conservatives of Warrington) which stands on the dining table at Walton records, by the largest majority (776) ever obtained in the constituency. He retired in 1892 and died in 1894, leaving no family by his first wife, but having a son and two daughters by his second. marriage That son is of course the present baronet, who, born in 1867, was sent to Mr. Poles's private school at Eversley, in Hampshire, whence he went to Eton in 1880. Dur- ing the four years he stayed there he was mere or less of a" wet-bob," but he never cared very much about boating or cricketimg, as he had imbibed a passion for hunting from his earliest days, and was allowed to follow hounds when only five or six years old. Uhon leaving Eton he was sent to a priv- ate tutor near Sawbridgeworth for a few months, and he was " finished," from the educational point of view,by a tutor at borne. During his father's life- time he hunted, principally from a lodge near Tarporley, with the Cheshire and managed the Covert Fund, of which he was for some time secre- tary. He would, in all probability, be hunting with the Cheshire still but for the mere chance ot his having gone with his cousin to see sport with the Fitzwilliam. This visit happened to coincide with the death of Mr. Tom Fitzwilliam, in con- sequence of which hounds did not go out, so Sir Gilbert and his cousin determined to have a few days with the Belvoir. The Duke of Eutland had just intimated his intention of givior, .up the titular mastership of the famous pack, and tsir Gilbert was quite casually asked to take office. The un6rtaking was an arduous one, as, apart from t.le prestige of the Belvoir, this was the first time the pack had been out of the Manners family, but Sir Gilbert decided to accept the offer, and no one who has hunted with these hounds during the last four seasons will suggest that a better choice could have been made The first thing that Sir Gilbert had to do was to build himself a house and stables, and he selected as a site Woolsthorpe, which is at the foot of Belvoir and on the boundary of Leicestershire and Lincolnshire. He is somewhat proud Of the fact that while the house, not begun until May, was ready for occupation by the begin- ning of the hunting season, stabling for sixt3- eight horses was completed in even less time, and it is there that he spends the winter, relieved by occasional flying visits to Walton. Althougn courteous in his demeanour he has the credit of keeping his field in good order, but the Belvoir, one is glad to know, is not much troubled with the galloping snob who is in such unwelcome pro- minence elsewhere.

With cab-hunting beginning in August, Sir Gil- bert has not much time for shooting, though be is a good shot, especially at partridges, of which there are plenty on the Walton estate; and perhaps his greatest amusement, after hunting, is paying visits to the principal horse shows, at which his services as a judge are in great request, as he has a rare eye for a horse, though he cannot often officiate in the hackney and pony classes, since he is so frequently an exhibitor. He is a very smart whip, too, and it is a treat to see him handle a pair of light-hearted young hor-es that have not often been in harnes before on the somewhat devious road from Wai- rington to Walton. it is refreshing, also, in these days when so many people seem to find every other country more agreeable to live in than their own, to hear from Sir Gilbert that he has only once crossed the Channel, and that on a brief visit to Pats. Nor must it he supposed that because he is so fond of horse and hound he neglects the duties which a position such cs his entails. He has never eared to seek the safe seat in the House which Warrington would unquestionably afford him, but he is chairman of the local Conservative Associa- tion, and he and his sisters are zealous in the cause ,which their father served so well and so long.— " World."

CROSFiELD.

The wedding took place on the 27th October at the Cathedral. Bombay, of Miss Aileen H Crosfield, daughter of Mr John Crosfield, J.P., of Walton Hall and Captain Cecil Moncrieff e ales, of the 41st Do- gra.s, and recently of the 2nd Punjaub Infantry, ot which latter regiment be wore.the uniform. The ceremony. was conducted by the Venerable Arch- deacon Hill. The bride, who was given away by Mrl W L Harvey, C.-.,. wore an ivory Chinese satin brc- cade dress, cut with a Watteau train and trimmest with Limerick lace. _ The neck and sleeves were of tucked chiffon, and a fall of accordian-pleated chif- fon in front was fastened at the shoulder with a knot of orange blossom. A wreath of the same flowers and tulle veil completed her costume. Miss Constance Crosfield, who attended her sister as bridesmaid, wore a dress of cream MOUSSelille soie and lace. Her hat was of pink fancy straw trimmed with roses and she carried a pink spray bouquet. Captain H B Pritchard, of the 22nd Madras Infantry, supported the bridegroom as best man, and there were also present Captain Locke, 2nd Bombay Grenadier?:; Captain A. li. Morris, R. A. 34. C.; Mr. ausrt, Black Watch ; and Mr Ballantyne, 19'h Bengal Cavalry. After the ceremony, which took place at eleven o'clock the newly-married couple and their friends repaired to Watson's Hotel, where Mrs Har- vey gave a wedding breakfast in her rooms, and ater on the happy pair lefs for Khandalla, a hill station in the neighbourhood of Bombay, where the honeymoon has been spent, the bride wearing a costume of pale mauve muslin with white feather hat. Note that it is in the actually spoken words of the former sufferer that the case is described. WITHIN easy reach of the Bedfordshire town of Dunstable lies the little village of Totternhoe, in a district of Roman remains, and old disused stone quarries which extend for miles underground, even, it is said, under Dunstable itself. Many visitors are attracted by these strange evidences of the past, being escorted through the subterranean workings by skilful and intelligent guides. A reporter attached to the Dunstable Gazette interviewed one of these guides the other day, Mr. Thomas Philpott, whom he found in his ideal cottage close to the foot of Totternhoe Castle Hill. It would have been well if Mr. Thomas Philpott had not spent so much of his time in these damp, dangerous quarries, for in after years—he is now sixty-six years of age—Sciatica and Acute Rheumatism seized him, with almost fatal results. "I became ill about two years arbm with Sciatica and Rheumatism," he said. "A doctor attended me for nearly twelve months, but at last I gave up all hopes of recovery. I first lost the use of my legs, then of my arms, then the agonising pains took me in the neck and back, and I became so weak and ill and helpless that it took two people to lift me in and out of bed; I could not even lift a limb." "That's quite true," said Mrs. Philpott, his kindly-looking wife. "Everybody said he could not possibly live long. We had to feed him on milk and invalids' food. He never touched an atom of solid food for nine or ten months." Mr. Philpott resumed: "I had. read in the papers about many people, suffering as myself, being cured by

" MUNICIPALITIES AT WORK?
Lecture in the Druids' Hall.

The third of the course of four lecture; nn " Q.stins of the Illy " was delivered in the Druids' Hall, Sankey- streer,last Thursday evening,when Mr. S D Shallard, of the Fabian Society sp,ke on " Municipalities at Work."

Mr Councillor BENNETT presided and in introducing the lecturer said the lectures would have a useful in- fluence in the town and he believed they could not fail to have a very beneficial influence indeed. The very first step towards' any improvement Di the existing conditions was that we 6houli thoroughly under- stand tnem. Eduction was the thing needed and these lectures were distinctly educational rather than controversial in their character. The subject that night was one which particularly appealed to him. He had had seven years experience of 'municipalities at work, and the result of the work bad been encouraging. One could not help feeling that there were maby thinks which were dis‘ppointing and die-illusioning, but on the whole from what be had seen he thought they were justified in hoping for great things by the working of municipalities in this country. Complaints were frequently made as to the ability or want of ability which sometimes distieguished some of their representatives, but what he wanted to amphasise was that the remedy lay in the hands of the peopre and it rested with them to send men to the C3uncil who would represent them and see that the policy they believed in was carried cut on sound and rational lines. They sometimes heard it said that certain men on the Council had axes to grind but his experience tauebt him that such complaints were -greatly exagger- ated. Warrington was served vary well on the whole by its Town Councii and h 3 believed it would compare very favourably with any ether in the country. (Hear, hear), They were looking forward to new developments of municipal activity. They had had ex- perience in Warrtneton of the control of the gas: and water supply and many other ordinary matters:which came within the scope of municipalities and he thought taey had lo,era tolerably well satisfied with the way they bad been conducted. They were shortly Co have the electric light and that was .10 be followed by electric tramways: (Hear, hear.) Tba most discouraging fea- ture in the situation was that extremely absurd proposal to appoint a committee on municipal tracing. It was entirely uncalled for bee ruse when a town wanted to undertake any new municipal work it was obliged to go to Parlia- ment for powers. Cerporations did not want any semi trary limitations. (Hear, hoar.) Let each municipality decide every question on its merits, and then apply to Parliament for the necessary power to carry it into effect. Be trusted that the Committee which had neen appointed on municipal trading, would hive the wisdom to decide not to place any check on municipal progress. (Hear, hear.) Referring to some of the possibilities of municipal work he referred to the fact that Manchester and Bradford were proposing to have their own collieries. He thought if it was a proper thing for a Corporation to supply gas it was quite loeical for that Corporation to have its own coal aupply for the making of gas. (Hear, bear.) Tnere was also no reaFon why if it was right for a Cor- poration to supply wirer it should net also supply beer. (Laughter.) He did not make that euegestion in a jocular way for he believed it was quite possible for the Corporation to control tbe public houses et the town. (Hear shear.) That in hi opinion was the best solution of the temperance question. The- licenses would then be in the hands of toe public an.i worked for the public good. If it were also right and logicsl for a corporation to condemn insanitary property he did not see why they should not have newer to erect houses which would not only be sanitary and sightly but fit for civilised beings.' (Hear, hear). Then if it were right for a Corporation to have parks for the delight of tlie people in summer he did not see why there should not be winter gardens for the people in winter. (Bear, bear.) Mr. SIULLAED then delivered his lecture on" Munici realities at Work." He said we did not always coneider what we owed to the great Municipal Reform act of 1835 which swept away the old corrupt and inefficient bodies which governed our towns. Ile gave examples of the mal-administration which obtained prior to the peesine of the act. The growth of municipal bodies was thuched upon and it was pointed out that in this country they new administered property valued at be- tween £300,000,000 and £400.000,000 This pre perry would, of course, be valued at considerably more if it were in the hands of private companies, for whereas the tendency with private companies was to set a high value upon their properties, municipalities immediately commenced to pay off the sinkine funds and reduce the capital value. IQ the control of gas and water undertakings, tramways and other public works It had been proved beyond doubt that municipalities were able to conduct them cheaper and more efficiently than private companies. By controlling the water sup- ply, municipalities had been able to reduce the price, purify the supply and raise the wages and shorten the hours of the servants employed. (applause.) There , were now only 150 private water companies in this country, whereas there were over 700 municipal water supplies. (Haar, hear) The Lectusee flowed the great advantages to the public which had followed the munini,pelisation of tramways in various cities and , to ses. Referring to the distribution of the profits of munieinalities,the lecturer stated that London had spent £12,000 on open-air music in its parka ; Edinburgh had provided an aitronomical observatory and a college; Glasgow a beautiful winter palace and family horn's, where widows and widowers c mid live with their chi - dren ; Bradford and Manchester, free gymnasiums and swimming baths ; Nottingham, tiplen.)id libraries and a municipal university ; Liverpool, free lectures in the Proton Hall; Londorngrew spplenfles and grapes in its gardenia and gave them to the hospitals and mar- , monies of the inetr )pelie; Bristol owned its own docks, and Warrington, he was elad to say, le o the way witli a muoicipal must utn and library. ( appleuse. ) The lecturer said most of the municipal work he MA alluded to was distributive work,hut mu, i• cipalirie, were now fineine it to /he r alvantage too" tit or own ‘,mk wiLhout the aid of contractors. Ex- perience of municipalitina had taught them that they ceold do their own work cheaper, more efficiently and econoinis'idle than letting it eu, to contractors. Most Cerperrt cans had Cow a Building or Wciki Com- mittee which undertook alt k rids of werk required by mueicipalities. The Birmiee ham Corporation's Build- hes C mmitee had built cottages, .cheols and a library for the people employed on their waterwerks in Wales and the London County Ceuncil had saved thousands oh pounds by doing their own works. Reference vs as also made to the suecessf el farming carried on by the Croydon Cernoration rind the supple of stem Hired milk by the St. Helens Corperatir n, which, bed had th effect according to the testimony of the medical office of h-alth in re toeing the infantile death rate, Tha advlsability of establishing municipal bakeries wa alluded to

div.head: WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB A Successful Year.
div.p: WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB A Successful Year.

The Committee Room of the Warrington Litoral Club was well filled on Monday evening oa the occasion of the annual meeting of the Club. In the absence of the President through illness, the chair was occupied by Ccurcillor 'Manion. Amongst those present were : Mr T Birchall, J.P., Councillor Peacock, Messrs John HArrison, S J Beaman, Joseph Albinson, William Bibby, 8 Dunb)bbin, T Critchley, James Strange, John Worrall, G Beard, and Thomas Pemberton (hou secretary). . Two letters of apology for non-attendance were read. Mr. Arthur U. Crosfleld (the esteemed president) wrote from Hoylake •• lam very provoked and very 7disej appointed at being prevented attending to-morrow'ri.' annual meeting at the club. I wrote Mr Tinnioe yestets" day ricking him if he would kindly take my place. The fact is that for the last few days I have been on the sick list, and in the doctors' hands, and the faculty forbid me undertaking any evening engagements of any kind proton. Will you please tell all our friencs how very sorry L am that for this -reason I shall not have the pleasure of meeting them to-morrow ? lam sure you will have a satisfactory meeting because of the excellent report you will have to give of the yeat'a working. May our club continue to gain in prosperity socially arid in influ- ence politically so as to put all oast records in the shaee !" The Mayor (Alderman Roberts) wrote : "Please apologise to my fellow-members of the Liberal Club for my absence from to-night's meeting, and kindly express my best wishes for the continued .prosperity of the club and of all its subscribers."

div.head: REPORT AND BALANCE SHEET.
div.p: REPORT AND BALANCE SHEET.

Mr PEMBERTON (hon. Secretary) prilented the annual report and statement of accounts. The report after mferring to the attendances at committee meetings, state:l that the rules drawn up in 1863 had from time to time been altered and arnencled, and the committee thought it desirable that the rules, as they at present stood, should be reprinted, revised, and submitted for approval at thst meeting. Great interest had been dis- played in the billiard handicaps, and bowling mains,and also in the pleasant smoking concerts Leld in the nark winter saeuths. They Were just commencing th.lr Christmas billiard handicap, tor which there were 134 entries, and he was pleAsed to tell them that their worthy President had already sent him a chr que for the prizes. (Applause.) The year financially had been a good one. The mennberbhip of the club was about the same. The new club which ban been opened by the opposition party had made no difference to them and he did not think they bad anything to fear as long as they made theit own club pleasant and comfortable. (Applause) The finances showed a profit of £34 03 51 on the year's worhing. Mr J WORRALL moved the adoption of the report and said it was a very flattering one, and th 3 club was in a very prosperous condition. Mr DIINBOI3BIN seconded, and it Was agreed to. MB. A. H CROSPIELD RE ELECTED PRESIDENT, MR. BIRCHALL AND THE WAR.

The CTIAIRISiN proposed the re-electices of Mr. A. U. Crosfield as president. He observed that they all re- gretted his inability to be present, and wished Lim a Opecay recovery to health and art nge h. (Hear. hear.) He could only say, in reviewing the history of the club, that its present position compared very favourably with its .pesitinn at any time in its history. They had excel- lent r fficers, and as chairman of the committee, he was bound to say that they had never had a more busioees- 'lke, enthusiastic, and better committee. (Hear, beer.) Every member had made h's utmost endeavour to further the interesta of the club and the interests or Liberalism, through the club; in Warrington. They had been specially fortunate in. having Mr Crosfield as pres'e dent. (Hear, hear.) He had done everything, and pre- bably more than any other man they could have Felected coadd poosibly have done. He had supported the club under all circumstances since he was connected with it, and it had always been a pleasure to approach him upon any matter if they could show him that it was for the benefit of the club and party.. tie had helped them handsomely, and they were fortunate in having him as their president. He lied great pLasure in proposing his re-election: (Applause.) Mr. BIRMIALL saki he had very great Drasure in seconding the resolutim. He endorsed the remar.s made concerning Mr. Crosfield. The Crcss lds had always ta.,en a strona ar:cl faithful body of helper.; to the Liberal party in Warrington, It was a great chsapp Antment to him (Mr. Birchall) that he was ir.disposed in London at the time of the election. He was able, however, to get a member of the other perry to abstain from voting. It d d nor, however, affect the result. He looked very eseerly, the morning tollowing the polling day for the reault. ' He was disappointed, but it was no mote than he expected, and as long as the infernal scarlet fever remained they would do no better. He did not kn rar whether if he had heee in Warrington to say all he had tc say that it would have helped them, this was tee most ignominious war that England bad ever entered upon. To his mind it was the bitterest and blackest chapter in our netional history, an when he heard of the burnisue of farms and the turning out of women and ciiildren on tue veldt of Soath Afriea, the fienting of women and children, and the destruction of their homes, it made his blood boil. There e cuid, how- ever, be a change before long, and her hoped they would all live to see it. (Hear, hear.) With regard to Mr. Crosfield, there was no man be (Mr. Irrchall) would sorrier support than him. He knew the President's erandather and he watt a staunch L The Cres- fields stuck to them manfully. He coneratulate the members on the pa es, nt condition of the club. He would with far a lit he more ocue.atiolel kfluenc in the principles of Liberaltam. There never was more need for reauneh eeberala to come to the front and plainly declara their opinions in political matters. (Applauie.) .Tile mot On was unanimously carried

div.head: FREE CHURCHES SIMULTANEOUS MISSION. , The Missioner for Warrington.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES SIMULTANEOUS MISSION. , The Missioner for Warrington.
"Reception" at Bold-street Schoolroom

It is now generally known that in February of next year a simultaneous mission ig to be held throughout the country by the Evangelical Free Churches. Toe subject has been engaging the anxious attention of the Warrington and District Free Church Council for some months past and much thought and lalecur have been given to the preliminary preparations. Tue general idea of the mission is to bring all the churches into line in one great effert to win men for Christ, by bringing the Gospel invitation within the reach of everybody, high and low, rich or poor, not only in the towns exd cities of the land, but also in the villages and hamlets. The missioner appointed for Warrington by the National Executive in London is the Rev. John Gould, of Cam- bridge, chairman of the East Anglia District. Mr. Gould has been called a riding preacher, from the fact tl:a,t he is one of the very few who in these dare work their circuits on horseback, after the faahion of toe early Methodist preachers. Although Mr. G )uld is net known in Warrington he has in the inaibt of Li; circuit labours conducted many successful mis,ions in large towns, and has been consniciously successful in East Anglia. The Mission services will extend from February 16:h to 26:h, 1901, inclusive, and be held in Bold-street Chapel, which has bt:en unanimously selected by the Free Church Council as being the most central and Con- venient. The venous departments of work, such as "Cahvassing and Visitation,"Printing and Advcri,ising,' "Devotional." "Finance," and the fortnation of a unit-d choir under the leadership of Mr. Walter Brough. have been relegrced to a number of sub-committees, and these committees have already commenced their labours. Sun- ay last, was observed in the Free Churches of the town for the purpose of directing the special attention of the congregations to the mission.

An aggregate meeting ot Christian workers, represent- I In all the Free Cnurches of the town, was held in Beld- street schoolroom on Tuesday evenieg, when the R3V. John Gould, the missioner appointed for Warrington was preeent, and had a hearty reception. Light refresh- ments were served from 7 to 8 p.m. A meeting was subsequently held. The Rev John Yonge, president of the ‘Varrington and District Free Church Connell, pre- sided, and there were also present :—Revs Theedor Bleh'los C 11 Hocken, H G Roberts (Wesleyan), J F slatthews. J T Sctiofield, J 8 Hughes (Baptist). J Milne (Prestyterian), E 1' Reed (Recormei Free Cnurch), C Finch (Primitive Methodist) ; Councillors James Evans, S Ellison, Messrs S B Stringer. A II Dunn, Hawthorn, i D.le. Barton, Williams, I Barlow, J J,Houghten. W He ley, and Jes'pe Meunfield. The CHAIBM4.I4 in the c.a.t:se of some introtuetory re- marks said he felt it to be a very great honour that it should fah to his let as president of the Warrington Free Church Coioncil to -preside over that very interesting meeting. His thouget tney migitt fairly take that meet ing as a sign and taken for good. He did not remernher any preliminary Meeting in connection with any prc- jected mission io Warrington being attended by such a large and representative gathering of the various local Free Churches as they had that ni,,ht. He trusted that the influ-ince of the meeting would spread through them to the churches with which they were connec ed and Chat there might be awakened amongst them a great and devoilt interest in the work they had in prospect. It was One of the most important meetings held in the history of the Free.Cnurches in Warrington. They were mot together for the purpose of inaugurating their share in that town oP.the great evangelistic mission which was to be held throughout the country in the month of February next year. After a reference to-the evange- listic missions whim] had been held in the town in recent years, some promoted by particular churches and others by the unitei free churches, but the projected m'stion was not den orenational or local in its character but it was a national an I netted mission and it was intended to be practically simultaneous throughout the kingdom. It was a unique thing altogeth4, and he ventured to think that in scheme was one which had not been rivalled in the history of the country. They believed the idea of th mission came to them from God Himself, and was first given te the mind of the Rev Di mills Law, the secretary of the National Federation of Free Church Counci:s, and when that gentleman brought the matter Deters his Council they accepted it and gave a great deal of consideration to the preparation of she enter- prise. The united ;elision had for its object the preaching of the gospel to the nation and b •g,inning the new century with new work for Jesus Christ. He veatured to think that it weuld aff ird a aplendid soect,iele for this nation. Toe Free Churches bad been criticised about their divisions, their sectarianism and aloofness from one another -and he feared there had been only too much Cause for it—bat in this happy and blessed rnissi m they were going to come together as they had never Coale before. (Ap- plause.) He believed this aimutaneous mission would be strong in i's influence npon the wh "le nation from the tact of its witty. It was a uni.ed movement for Christ against' toe fore's of., sin, againsc toe prevalent unbelief eel terrible indiffer7.erace which existed in the masses of the people of this country • It was a united movement to save the people, It was a terrible thing when they came t think of it that tne m-j wity of the people of this cedetry had ceased Lo worseip Gol. The bIICC!.B of the mission depended to a far e roarer exteet than under ordinary circtrnstanees upon tas devoted enthusiastic work of all the enurches wno were ce:. nected with it. An the teachers in their echotla. al, he local preachers belonging to the churches, their Cnristian Eadeaveurers and members of churche3 must seek to find simn personal part which they can take in the promotion of this mission. The leaders would need to be eupporte i most loyally, and it %you'd have to be a miaeleno the rank and file as well a; of the nlE:eels of the •ceirions free chili chei. Tee churches must to rescued from their pres; nt apathy, and indifference. AEI mission wonli inveeve a large_amount of preparatory work, end tie h •pod Inc wai a large nointier of whom had been secured - would make up their minds to do seinetteng for tile mi,siou. Every liaise in the town had to tie visited about this mission net only once or twice but perhaps three or four times. That meant a very large amount of work, but if they wished to reach i and rouse the town that was tit' only way it could be done, (Hear, beat).

Ttie Rev 0 H HOCKEN in introducing the RevJ Gould, said he wa4 sure, they were rtsolved in tipir heArts to carry out the details ot organisation as though the whole nisSiot depended entitely upon themselves. (App'ause.) de had had some associstilo with Mr Gould in mission work in times past aod he felt certain that Mr Gould would be a genial leader in this great mission work. (11Par, bear)_

He a surrd them that he was not there by any see k.ng f his own.
