div.head: EXAMIN EH.
div.p: THE EXAMIN EH.
NOVEMBER 23RD 1900.
THE Irish Nationalists will Ireland and the Sessions. probably not attend West-

minster for the shor session next month. There is nothing surprising in this move. The attendance means expense, and the business is one in which few Nationalists sympathise, and in no way concerns the affairs of Ireland. There is a convention fixed for December 11th, and it is more important for Irish M.P.'s than voting money to continue the war. The terms of the resolution in which Irish members areoadvised not to attend are not, however, such as we can approve. The war is doubtless " detest- able "in some of its aspects, as all wars are. But we cannot admit that it was "begun in greed" inasmuch as the Boers invaded British territory, or that it has been carried on "with revolting barbarity," or that British members are either politely or correctly described as "British criminals." These rhetorical excesses injure the attitude we can quite understand that Irishmen may conscientiously take up. They injure their own cause, however, when they pervert the facts, and extol the virtues of the Boers at the expense of 'their own compatriots under arms and at the expense of truth. Hundreds of Irish soldiers in the field can give their testimony as to whether "revolting barbarity" has been practised by them or by English and Scotch troops. We could under- stand the reluctance of the Irish members to sanction the war in any way, and if they resisted every vote about it, or declined to attend Parlia- ment whilst it Was being discussed, their conduct would not be open to serious objection. But we must protest against a Parliamsntary minority styling the rest of the House of Commons ';criminals," and then claiming that refusing to associate with them is dignified. It is from these is criminals " that the Irish members are hoping to win Home Rule, and they are well aware that a section of these members has suffered political loss and deprivation because of alherence to the cause of Ireland and a desire to promote Irish views. Gratitude is rare in politics, but an English member who has been a consistent Home Ruler, and has been busted accordingly, might have expectecllbetter treatment. Tea Unionist doubts his patriotism, and if he supports the war the Nationalist calls him a "criminal." This being the temper of the Irish members, they are better away from Westminster, where their presence could cause only turbulence and distraction. The Irish Unionists, on their part, will be compelled to attend, and they are troubled with a little matter of their own. Some of them are re- joicing that Mr. HORIOE PLUNKETT has been de- prived of his seat because he appointed a National- ist to a position on the Agricultural Board. We donot sympathise with them. A spirit of exclu- siveness is had, whether it is manifested by one section in Ireland or by another. Tho behaviour of the extreme Unionists almost puts them on a par with the extreme Nationalists. It enables everybody to see what difficulties there are in con- nection with Irish government,and how impossible it is to "kill Home Rule with kindness "—or, in- deed, we may say, withlanything at all. We must either give it or live in a state of perpetual CO3- flict. Another difficulty is as to Mr. HORACE PLUNKETT'S seat. He cannot hold his present office for long and be without a seat. The Govern- ment will not fled a seat for him if he is going to give assistance to Mr. T. W. RUSSELL'S landlord expropriation campaign, and Mr. RUSSELL may have to determine whether henceforth he shall call himself a Unionist or a Liberal. In the event of another Vice-President being required to take Mr, 110 RAGE PLUNKETT'S place, he is Sure to be a Unionist of a less genial and progressive type.

Under these conditions, it seems that Ireland is with us still, a thorn in the flesh,an inconveniences a political disability. This fact alone is worth the attention of the wise, and it is the duty of the Imperialist to regard it with the severest logic.

AN intimation is made The Hospital Inquiry —as Expected. that the report of the Hospital Commission will be practically a vindication of the army authorities. Some defects and evils will be admitted,accounts will be described as exaggerated, personal narratives will be declared to be imperfect and unreliable, and the Medical Corps will be com- plimented upon the energetic way in which it com- bated with enormous difficulties. The country will not be astonished at such a finding. It was the one intent from the first. The inquiry was resisted and resented,and the organisation of it was such as to render any independent, unbiassed and exhaustive conclusion improbable, if not impossi- ble. Primarily it was not an accusation against the doctors at all, and yet the inquiry has been conducted as to vindicate a noble profession from the charge of inhumanity, and the Medical Corps from accusations of neglect and incapacity. The original charge was in general terms, and the facts laid bare will suffice to prove it. There was inex- cusable neglect, there were needless suffering and fatalities; there were avoidable epidemics ; there were insufficient beds, nurses, necessbriesp and comforts. These things did not occur at all the hospitals, and at every part of the theatre of war, and they could not be all placed upon the shoulders of the Medical Corps. The transport allowed was under the local commanders and not the medical authority. The railway services were controlled by the military and not by the medical authority. The absence of the necessary beds and supplies was not always easily traceable to anY" body. The Government at home sent out the beds, stores, necessaries, and medical comforts. But many of them never reached their proper place. Hundreds of soldiers died of enteric fever who ought never to have had fever at all. They died in camps to which they ought never to have been sent. They died for want of proper care and food. The pressure was too great, and no attemPt , seems to have been made to prevent the heavy load which followed the pressure by such instructions from home or such hearty co-operation between the military and medical authorities on the spot !Al would have been effective. The military exigencieS received every attention, and the hospital exigen" cies were not promptly dealt with. A Polite white' wash was expected, and it seems to be forthcom- ing. The Commissioners seem to have begun their inquiry as if they were to investigate a definite charge against a definite body, and one so inher" ently improbable as to give them a strong bias in favour of the accused. The result was foreseen. The Medical Corps is acquitted of inhumanity, but it was never charged with it. It is said to have been making the best of the means at its disposal; and this also was never challenged. But if the report would say that the epidemics of typhold were unavoidable, that the mortality was to be expected, and that the beds and hospital arrange" ments could not have been better under the olr" cumstances, we shall take leave to doubt the justice of any finding. The blame must rest upon the War Office, upon the generals in command, and to a much slighter degree upon the ArmY Medical Corps. The inquiry was not t 3 (31'11'1111a charges against the latter. It was to discover the truth, and to distribute the blame in an impartzia way. Failure to do this is lamentable.

A writer in the" World "who has been insPecte. ing Walton Hall lets fall the remark that "it Is. situated within three miles of Warrington--; town which Ruskin, had he ever passed that W3J would assuredly have condemned for having artistic beauty." We have fortunately esnaPc, Ruskin's condemnation and can only suffer ranel the reproach cast at us by a" lesser light itle• as the " World's " correspondent. Our artistict beauty is undoubtedly a minor—if liCd minus—quantity, but the deficiency someday be made up. Is there not the " Dream- ,of a Warringtonian ' in which the town's artistic beauty is a distinctive feature? And dreams some- times come true Unfortunately for thnso esthetically-inclined there are other things more ' urgent in Warrington than the cultivation of .Arttsi We are said to be 50 years behind in munlclP.o, government, and until the completion of such bit; schemes as electric lighting, tramway's, etc., reis,, us to the level of progressive towns, Art will War to remain in the background. It has its ardenive supporters, :however, and what little is possi/Pd is being done to relieve the drab monotony sc angular, ugliness of this typical manufacturing town.

Comment is being made on the fact that tll9 price of horses of almost every type has gone ti That, of course, is largely due to the war; but, electricity and motor-cars had made any iniPiw. mon the advance would not have been to anytl3.ll3l: like the extent it is. For example, an oranOT.l horse to-day costs 50 per cent. more than it übto eighteen months ago, and it is clear that, as "tr. war is holding ous,—if the motor omnibus iul-ja tors are ever to get in—they have had a apleil‘%t chance ot obtaining business. It may be said tlitio' the motor omnibuses cost a great deal of menel build, and that they could not be turned °op quickly; but it is equally true that you caTli 0 hasten the growth of a horse, an' the considerable time must elapse before, -na, present tightness of the market can be relieve:A In these circumstances the wonder is it' of alike for the carriage of goods OIL to passengers, no serious attempt has been Ouncli use the new force for conveyance. It is 131 tbe, cleaner, and more certain in its effect, al?`l4 et avoidance of horses would mean a great savitio of space in the streets. The advance in the ont i 3 horseflesh is not an advance which, once done with. Omnibus horses last oDly a ve.,Yhave years, and it is unlikely that the prices $11";„iale gone down to their old level before fresh sl3,7lced. have to be bought to replace those now et°' Indeed, there is a constant sale going otblittte doubt the companies in London made a nice .;bOY sum by the sale of horses for the war, but have more than lost that advantage since.

The Warrington Liberal Club is maintaining its Prosperous condition and one has no difficulty in believing that the dark days of the past are gone never to return. Every year for some time now,a handsome profit has been made,and notwith- standing recent expenditure the same satisfactory result was announced at the annual meeting on Monday evening. Only one thing of importance is there with which we are not entirely satisfied, and that is the amount of work done for Liberal- ism. To a very great extent the club is a working- men's social club, and merely the nominal head- 'quarters of the Liberal party in Warrington, in- stead of being the pivot of things political and progressive. The first rule of the Club is "to pro- mote Liberal principles," but nothing is ever done which is at all likely to achieve this desirable object. Comfort and socia- bility are carefully attended to, but politics are neglected entirely. This is not being loyal either to Liberalism or the President of the Club. Mr. A. H. Crosfield, whose interests as Liberal candidate for the borough eught to be in the minds of the members he does so much for. We should like to see something in the nature of educational work started even if there does not seem any burning desire for it among the mem- bers. It is the duty of the management to "pro- mote Liberal principles," and until they make an attempt they will not have justified themselves in the least though they may be able to point to a cash balance and a large membership.

The publicans of Warrington are becoming very amenable to reason, and deserve every credit for BOtne of their recent actions. At the re- quest of the licensing bench they agreed t? abolish the pernicious system known as Riving the " long pull," and by doing so have lessened the sources of intemperance very con- siderably. This week they have decided not to give away any Christmas gratuities to customers, and are thus pursuing the course of action taken last Year. Like the " longpull," Christmas gratuities are a serious evil, putting, as they do, additional temptation to drink in the way of people ill- calculated to resist it. The firmness of the licensing bench hag, of course, much to do with spoch sensible decisions being come to by the licensed victuallers, but, on the whole, we think these much abused tradesmen merit sincere com- mendation for an honest desire to conduct their businesses in a manner the mom satisfactory to the authorities and the least harmful to the public.

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

Manchester's unpleasant experience is furnishing quite a useful object lesson for other provincial Municipalities. It has been announced during the Week in connection with other public bodies, many miles from Manchester that professional gentle- men who have seats in the local councils have re- tired from sub-committees because of its being pos- sible that their private interests may clash with those of the public. The announcements should be hailed with pleasure by everyone who is anxious for the maintenance of a bigt standard in public life. In most towns the business is no doubt carried on by men who in the main are really disinterested, and it is not at all likely that anything very dread- ful would happen from the .presence of solicitors and architects, for instance, on the sub-committees, Which deal with improvement -schemes, and pass plans for new houses and other property. On the other band, it 'is probable that in many instances their professional know- ledge would be of the greatest value to their colleagues. Yet there are those who think it iS better to avoid even the appearance of evil, and solicitors, surveyors, and architects havealready declined to serve on sub-committees. Under the •• circumstances they probably act wisely ; though it is a matter which it is possible to conceive of being pushed too far. Mr Vaudrey, who furnished the ex- ample upon which others have acted, resigned his seat on the Improvement Committee of the Man- chester pity Council against the well nigh unani- mous wish of his colleagues. He did it because there are certain transactions pending in connection with the Ship Canal in which he will be concerned for private individuals who are his• i Cliente. It s possible the same thing may happen to members of other town or city or district Councils and if every member of these bodies who may be placed ma deli- cate position between public duty and private in- terest is to he excluded in advance from commit- tees, many members will be unable to act at all.

Opinions of the medical journals do not carry so much weight and influence with them as they did once upon a time, when they had not begun to decry every habit we had formed and everything we did tor our own good, as we thought, and as they seemed not to think, but the" Lancet" makes up a little this week for unduly extolling the virtues of the " weed" last week, by taking a common sense view of the practice of what is universallyknowu as" treating," which it condemns. ." What is true for the Army,' it says,referring to theutterances of our Generale, "is true for those who live by labour, who need to spend wisely what they make, and who can only rise in the social scale by strength of character and self-denial," adding that "the prac- tice of ' treating ' is wholly bad. beeause it leads to casual drinking, a habit which lays the founda- tion of disease." It might have added, that it is the most insidious and most dangerous kind of drinking to the beginner, and the cause of more ot the evils resulting from intemperance than any other form of drinking known. If " treating " conld be 'stamped out immoderate drinking, to say the least, would be minced one-half, and drinking generally Would becomeiraore rare because less "respectable."

It is a damaging commentary on the methods of 'Our fruit growers that, with the markets absolutely glutted with home produce, great consignments being quite unsaleable,large quantities of American Baldwin apples and customers in our wholesale tzaarkets. This is because our growers do not attempt t 9 grade" their produce for the market, They A. 1 naply have it piled in a heap and shovelled anyhow ' Into anything that will carry. Consequently,buyers prefer the carefully selected produce of foreign origin, neatly and properly packed in barrels of uni- form size, which is easy to deal with, and tempt- ing to all classes of buyers. Yet our growers have ihe,mscience to complain of preferential treatment to Ihe foreigners ! It remains to be said, however, that t'ne American apples are not selling at a price that can pay the senders, The glut appears to be universal, and none really gain by it but the re- tailers and consumers. At the same time it affects all classes of fruit.

It is well for the public to know that the increase in the revenue of the Customs and Excise last quarter, as compared with that of the correspond- ing period of last year, does not mean that there hae been an increased consumption of dutiable articles. It is wholly due to the higher rates of duty levied, since in most cases there has been a decrease in consumption. Possibly people have been drinking less tea and spirits than usual, but the smokers have, apparently, been indulging more freely; a point that may be taken to indicate that the working classes are, 3o far, fairly prosperous. Whether the prosperity will be maintained through the winter is rather doubtful. Careful observers are expecting trouble, especially in the mining dis- tricts, owing to the sleekening demand for coal, and the influx into the labour market of the troops returning from the war. At any rate, of the dutiable articles taken tor consumption during tbe quarter just ended, tobacco alone shows an increase ill the Excise revenue.

Geceral Sir Relivers Buller has this week had a m.ost enthusiastic welcome in Exeter, the capital of rim own county, which will serve to remind other cithis and towns of what is expected from them when their respective heroes and soldiers of the line return from tile scene of their recent exploits 'n South Africa. So far as Sir Redvers Buller is concerned, he is of the type that Tommy Atkins ally loves. Fearless in danger yet ever cautious JO safeguard the lives of his men, no General, prob- h.b!y has bad a more difficult task during tbe hosti- lities in South Africa, and when the history of this regrettable and terribly costly campaign comes to be written, it is trusted that justice will be meted

out to those, including General Buller who have come in for a lirge amount of criticism, perhaps justifiable under the circumstances and at the time, but not upheld by subsequent events and unques- tioned explanations.

What has become of ex-President Kruger's coach is a question that has been raised while Kruger is on his starring tour off the shores of France. This coach was known to he an elaborate turn-out, de- corated in all the colours and with all the devices emblematic of the late Republic, d lined through- out with pale blue satin. It was built in London, and was delivered in Pretoria to a citizen of Exeter, Mr E Gould, who has lately returned home. Mr Gould wrote to Lord Roberts, an inquiry respec- ting the whereabouts of the splendid chariot, and has received the following reply : Dear sir, I am desired by Lord Roberts to acknowledge the re- ceipt of your letter, and to inform you that Mr. Kruger's carriage is still et his house in Church-st., Pretoria.—Yours faithfully, Stanley.

It is perfectly true that pianos have at last found their way into a workhouse far the use of the in- mates, but before the reader is overwhelmed by the announcement., and begins to exclaim" What int the world next 1" let it be added that the iustrusaents cost the ratepayers nothing. Dr. Ley, a guardian and J.P. who takes a kindly interest in the Newton Abbot Workhouse and its ihmates,has issued a letter of thanks to four hundrGd and thirty-three sub- scribers to his fund for purchasing two pianos for the use of the poor people living in the house; the total cost of the subscriptions amounting to £4O 4s 2d. There are now three pianos, one for each sex, and one for general use.

div.head: LITNA.TICS AND IMBECILE&
div.p: LITNA.TICS AND IMBECILE&

The Clerk read a circular from the Local Government Board stating that the Board had itouel an order, copies of which were enclosed, directing that within 48 hours after the death of a lunatic in any Poor Law Institution notice of sucn death should be sent by the superintend- ing officer of the institution to the coroner of the district in which tine institution was situated.

Mr Norman said they had no lunatics in the Work- house, only imbeciles and yet this order put them under restrictions as if they were running an asylum. The Chairman said it was a matter which involved serious responsibilities, and they ought if possible, to send these pee* to the Inuatic asylum, as some of them were not fit to associate With ordinary inmates of a workhouse. This was a sealed order and seemed to give the Board no choice. The Clerk said it did not follow there would be an in- quest in each case. The coroner would decide whether an inquest was uecessary or not. Mr. Norman referring to the suggestion to send the whole of the imbeciles to the asylum said the difficulty was to get a doctor's certificate that would entitle them to entrance to an asylum. The Clerk said this order referred to lunatics ; if the medical officer did not certify the imbeciles as lunatics, the Master was not called upon to consider them as luna- tics.

The Master said there were five inmates certified under the Lunacy Act. Mr. Norman said the difficulty was to get a certificate certifying them lunatics fit for the asylum; if tho Board could get Rath certificates he would not hesitateto send the whole of them to the asylum. It was decided to defer consideration of the subject until the uttedicai officer and the master had made in- quiries. The Clerk reported having received a circular letter from Mr CE Speakman, clerk to the Nantwich Union enclosing copies of resolutions passed by the Board, and asking him to lay them before the Runcorn authority That in the opinion of this Board the time has arrived for the provision of institutions for the reception of imbecile a•id epileptic inmates of Union Workhouses and the Beard approves of action being taken by the Unions of the County or the Local Government Board to carry this into effect. Also that the clerk do communi- cate with the several Unions in the County with a view to a conference baing held at Crowe for the purpose of considering the subject of the foregoing resolution, and, if it is thought desirable of further consideration what steps shall be taken. On the proposition of Mr Norman the Board expressed approval of the resolution and raolved that if a confer- ence were decided upon to send representatives.

The Clerk reported -t-ti;-t- the School Attendance Com- mittee had that day adopted new bye-laws. The age of exemption was raised from 13 years to 14 years. With regard to the distance from which a child should be compelled to attend school, this bad been altered from two miles to one and a half miles ,tap to nine years of age, and over nine years, three miles. The standard of eximption had been raised from the fifth to the sixth, and the standard for partial exemption remained the same—the fourth standard. The committee had added a special clause to apply to agriculture to the effect that any child between 11 and 13 years shall be allowed to absent itself from school between the end of March and 'the middle of May, and again from the middle of August to the beginning of October if it was shown thai it bad attended 250 times during the year. The penalty clause for non-compliance with the bye-laws had been altered so as to make the penalty 20s for each offence in- stead of ss. The bye-laws would C3lllO into force as soon as they were approved oy the Education Department. In reply to Mr. Mclntyre, Ur. Woodward said the committee adopted the bye-laws unanimously after con- siderable discussion. This was the whole of the business.

Warrington Field Club. it the fourth meeting of the session Mr J L.Stone F.L.S., of Birmingham, delivered a lecture entitled "Timber from a botanical standpoint," illustrating the subject with the specimens recently presented by him to the Museum—representing about 180 kinds from all parts of the world—and with a series of beautiful lantern slides, many of which were actual sections of the various timbers. The lecture was listened to with close attention, anti was especially valuable, since it embodied the results of many years' study by Mr Stone of timber both in its growth and when felled and dressed for use. Amongst the points—positive and negative— made by the lecturer, was that the rings seen in the section of a felled tree are associated with the annual leaf-fall, and that if the foliage be artificially stripped from a deciduous tree befre the summer is over a faint ring will record the circumstance, and that when a fresh lot of leaves has grown and fallen in the natural way in antumn'a further ring will be produced. Many attempts have been made to classify timber as timber—Mr Stone himself having been working at this subject for several years—but hitherto the results are merely negative; species cannot be certainly recognized by the grain or the section of the wood. Dealing with the question of varying solidity in timbers, he showed that it is not merely because the tissues are ein,er, out because in some there is a larger proporoon of mineral matter. The wood of a tree is really an accumulation of matter once alive but now dead ; the life of the tree being limited to the bark and its outgrowths. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr Stone on the proposition of Councillor Greening, seconded by Alderman J Shaw. i Green. Several members took part in the discusqon, and t is hoped that the in- terest aroused may stimulate the botanical mem- bers of the club to farther exertions until they attain as high a level as the entomological section. NATIONAL UNION OF TEACHERS.

On Saturday evening a special general meeting of the Runcorn and Widnes Teachers' Association was held in Victoria-road Board School, Runcorn. Mr J Brown presided, and there was a representa- tive attendance of members. The Secretary (Mr G S Smith), read letters received from Messrs. J H Yoxall, M.P., and Ernest Gray, M.P., and Dr Macna- Mrs, M.P, thanking the association for their kind congratulations on their -success at the general election. The meeting then considered and approved of the scheme 'for electoral district con- ferences referred to the local associations by the executive. Afterwards Mr R Lloyd, of Chester, delivered an address on" The Teachers' Provident Society," explaining its workings and the advan- tages of membership. An interesting discussion followed, and it was ultimately decided to estab- lish a branch in connection with the local associa- tion, the presant local members of the society to constitute the committee of management. A vote of thanks to Mr Lloyd for his able and instructive address, proposed by MT R Devonald, seconded by Mr F J Moulton, was unanimously carried, and the meeting terminated.

rates for this bridge scheme: Why had the Council not possible burden of £5OO per year on the provided the town with baths? Because they could not afford it, and yet baths would not have cost more than id. or 2d. in toe £on the rates. If these two were put before the ratepayers in competition with the bridge.the ratepayers would ask that all available funds should be put in these two projects rather than in ,:he speculative investment of the bridge, HA pointed out that when the recreation ground was taken in hand the financial prospects of the town were brighter than they were to-day. They had within the past few months received a communication from the Local Government Board which materially altered the aspect of things. How often bad they thought of the great advantages which would accrue from enlarging the boundaries of Runcorn, but if this £lO,OOO proved unremunerative, the prospect of including the outside townships would be put back half a century. Mr Taylor said from the commencement he had advc- cated investing money in the bridge because it would be one of the greatest blessings that could be conferred upon the town and he now supported the investment of £lO,OOO very strongly. He referred to the representa- tive character of the meeting of ratepayers that had suggested this sum, and said it included working-men with a stake in the town and taking that meeting as a guide, the people were in favour of £lO,OOO. Mr Wiswall predicted a second transporter bridge and then a per- manent bridge. He was delighted to hear it. He hoped Mr Wiswall would be a true prophet for he was sure the ratepayers. the shopkeepers, and property owners would be delighted if these bridges were needed to meet the requirements of Runcorn At the public meeting somebody made the assertion, which he was not justified in doing, that Mr Posnett waa the only one who was going to take shares in the company. If he (Mr Taylor) could get shares he pur- posed taking some because he was firmly convinced the oampany would pay. It was the duty of the Council to invest £lO,OOO. Mr Wilson also supported the resolution, because of the importance of having a member on the directorate of the company. It ban been said their representative would be of no value to Runcorn because he would be in the ratio of Ito 7or 1 to 9. He contended that the interests of Widnes and Runcorn were alike; what would benefit Widnes in the way of trade brought by the Transporter Briage would • also benefit Runcorn and he could safely assert that in 99 cases out of 100 the representatives of the two towns would stand shoulder to shoulder. The present monopoly of the London and North-Wes- tern Railway Company worked to the detriment of Run- corn. When they had a chance of improving that state of things they ought to do their best to do so, consistent with public safety. He believed the Council would do the right thing by voting £lOOOO for the bridge scheme, which was bound to be remunerative and the money in- vested would be a realisable asset.

Mr. Pritchard in supporting the reeolution pointed out the many advantages the Transporter Bridge had over the present means of communication. It was a low level bridge ; passengers would be carried instead of having to walk ; the journey would only take three minutes, and it would be a financial benefit to the com- munity as the single fare would )e fifty per cent. less than the present charge and the return fare 33 per cent. less. Towards the maintenance of the highway from the boundary of Halton to the railway station Cheshire County Council contributed £4OO per year, and surely this bridge, connecting two important counties and two important town was worth something in the £. The Council should take sufficient holding with the Transporter Company to en- title them to a public representative. Mr. Gatley said he thought it his duty as the repre- sentative of working men at election times and at this time to vote in favour at the £lO,OOO. The new bridge would be of indirect and direct advantage to the work- ing classes as pointed out by Mr. Dean. and after the decision of the ratepayers meeting he felt compelled to vote for £lO,OOO The amendment was voted for by Messrs Wiswall, Grise, Imison, Lightburn, Hewitt, Jones and Salkeld-7 The remainder of the Council voted against—lo, the Chairman declared the amendment lost.

Mr Imison characterised the calling of the ratepayers meeting as a weakness, and said there were not more than 60 persons cresent and ridiculed the idea of the Council taking the vote of that meeting as a mandate on the question. By calling that meeting the Council had seriously impaired tbe;.r efficiency as representatives. Mr Wiswall.—There has been a great deal said about this ratepayers meeting. (Laughter.) It was a very great disappointment to me.—(Laughter.) The Chairman: Don't travel outside the resolution, please. Mr. Lightburn said he had voted against the £lO,OOO, not because he did nst value the great advantage the bridge would bestew, but because he thought a repre- sentative was not worth an extra £5,000. The resolution was then put and carried by ten votes to seven,and the necessary agreement with the Company was sealed.

div.head: RUNCORN NOT ES
div.p: RUNCORN NOT ES
[By a Correspondent].

This week the town of Runcorn has been visited by the founder of the "Salvation Army," and very many of our folk availed themselves of the oppor- tunity of hearing and seeing the venerable General Booth, who as a man, stands by himself, eccentric and distinctive. General Booth's individuality has exerted an influence for good amongst the slums of the United Kingdom, and a large portion of the Continent, but it was evident that the heigli-day of Salvationism in Runcorn is past and gone, for apparently the large crowds that assembled were actuated more by curiosity than with sympathy for the cause. One does not want to be prophetic, but it would seem so to say that Tuesday last had the appearance at being the last brilliant effort in an effete cause, the last flicker before the candle dies out.

The Runcorn Rural District Council have agreed upon new and important bye-laws which affect the school children under their jurisdiction. The age of exemption was raised from 13 to 14 years, and the distance from which a child under nine years should be compelled to attend school was reduced from 2 miles to 11 miles, and for over nine years of age the distance was fixed at 3 miles. The standard of exemption was raised from the fifth to the sixth, and the standard for partial exemption remained the fourth. There was a special clause applying to agriculture, to the effect that any child between eleven and thirteen years shall be allowed to absent itself from school between the end of March and the middle of May and from the middle of August to the beginning of October if it had attended 250 times during the year. The penalty for non-com- pliance with the bye-laws was fixed at 20s for each offence, instead of 5. The bye-laws are to come into form when sanctioned by the Education De- partment,.

At last the tension is over awl the Runcorn Urban District Council have decided to invest .£lO,OOO in the Transporter Bridge undertaking. I can congratulate my,elf that the consummation has in some measure been brought about by the strong agitation in this column and other columns of the "Examiner." But in the bringing about of the re- sult much has come to light which is beyond the ordinary. Indeed the Transporter Bridge has been a factor of the greatest historic importance to the town,tor it has been the means—though why I fail to see the reason—of bringing the Liberal and Tory parties up to the mark. It has been the rock upon which the harmony of our local Parliament has split, and it will be seen from the vote in the matter that the die of politics has been cast and the town has entered upon an era of party govern- ment.

What the possibilities of that Government will be in the tuture one cannot foresee, and to enlarge upon them will not at present suit my purpose. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof, and my sufficiency is exemplified in my rejoicing. To one fact I would, however, call general attention, and that is the vindication of the character of Sir J T Brunner, our Liberal M.P., to which Mr Imison has given utterance. It will not be easily forgotten Mr Imison gave us all cause for indignation during the last electoral campaign by what Liberals were pleased to call an unwarranted attack upon Sir John and especially dealt with the interference of Sir John in lccal matters." Now, we see that Mr Imison almost unqualifiedly retracts, by the utter- ance of the following sentence at the recent sitting of the Urban District Council.—" The Council have irequently approached him (Sir John) upon far less important matters than this," Thus we have es- tablished that Sir John's "interference" is generally by invitation. As all good Liberals heartily cen- sured Mr, Imison when he attacked, so will they applauds now he retracts, and no one will regret that a source of friction between Mr. Imison and many of his personal friends is in great measure remove d.

Mr R A Naylor of Cuerden Hall, The!wall sent to the Clerk on the 19th inst a letter of twelve pages, the burden of which was that he was much obliged to the Council for having the tannery ditch cleaned out ; but the next day the pollution of it made matters very unpleasant. His coachman took a sample of the effluent with the result that be quite col- lapsed. On Monday last his house was worse than ever before experienced although the brook was not smelling very much. On Tuesday the brook and the whole tan- nery wcre reeking with the vilest odours and the coach- man's wife and boy were both made ill. On Tuesday,be understood, the inspector took a sample of effluent when the brook was fairly free from odour and any result from this would be practically useless. A good deal of putrid smell arose from the fleshings, which Dr. Adams had reported cause " a distinct smell nuisance." These were now distributed over a greater area and nearer the coachman's unfortunate dwelling. Then there were the two very smoky chimneys which seemed to convey the deadly turner for miles around. He was not surprised to hear that a little child had just died from diphtheria. Last winter there were 12 cases of this disease, four or five of which proved fatal, but like the present case they were hushed up and not the slightest effort made to discover the cause of the outbreak. Whatever now happened from this detestable stench, the Coun- cil would most surely be blamed for it The medical officer after much quibbling now , declared that the tannery nuisance and sewage were injurious to health, and with this definite statement trfore them he hoped the Council would rise to the occa- sion, and whether there wra only one cause or a. com- bination of causes, make full use of their powers, and let the people have the danger removed. The Inspector had said there was nothing wrong with the drainage of his (Mr. Naylor's) property, but if the Council found on minor investigation any such offence " pray take instant action, and for Heaven's rake let us not have , further delay Which might mean sickness and death." Mr. Naylor concluded with this sentence " I suppose the fight will now soon commence, and let me assure you I do not enter the cosflict with any ill-feeling towards you." The Inspector (Mr, Farrington), writing to the Clerk under date November 16Ar, with reference to the open ditch and cesspit situate in Waste-lane in Grappenhall and Thelwall, stated that he inspected the ditch and cesspit on the 15th just, and found that the ditch bad been cleared and scoured in a thorough and satisfactory manner, and the cesspit contained no solid matter ex- cepting a few inches of gravel and stones. Owing to the large volumes of flood water in the ditch he (the in- spector) declined to take a sample for analysis but took one to submit to the Council. Mr. Naylor had a man stationed on the spot who, he was intormed, took notes daily. Dr Adams said if he were to answer Mr Naylor's statements in reference to himself he should give them a direct traverse. He was down the thy the brook was cleaned out and there was no smell. Mr Naylor said there was an awful smell that day, but be (Dr Adams) could not detect it. It was a curious thing that the smell should devastate one set of people and leave the other set of people alone. Mr Woodward said there was a party through the village on the day named and they could not detect any of the objectionable smells mentioned. Inspector Farrington produced a sample of the diluent.

Mr Woodward examined it and said there was nothing objectionable about it. Inspector Farrington said the sample was taken seven days after the brook was cleansed. He had taken it as a curiosity for the Council,it was not quite a fair e ample to submit for analysis. Dr Adams suggestk d that when a sample was taken repr,sentatives of both Messrs Long and Mr Nas lor should be present to see it taken, This was agreed to.

REFUSING TO QUIT A WESTON HOTEL.

Joseph Allman, against whoei many convictions have been recorded, was tined by the Runcorn Mag- istrates on Tuesday, arid mulcted in costs up to the amount of lOs for refusing to quit the " Royal Oak," Weston.—Prisoner admitted being drunk but said he did not ask the landlord for anyth ug but a bottle of soda water.lle had received his drink trom the farmers when out with a thrashing machine, and wapted to lessen the effect.—The Bauch did not seem very much impressed with tile excuse. TRINITY CIIAPEL, WIDNES.

On Sunday the anniversary emcee; of the above chwel were preached by the Rev James Watkin, president of the Liverpool Free Church Council. In the afternoon a service of song was given, entitled "his mother's Portraio' There were g )od congre- gations at all services, the coiltrztioas being most satisfactory.
NEW GRAND MASTER OF CUESILIRE MASONRY.

The lion Alan de Tatton Egerton, M.P., having been appointed Provincial Grand Master of Ones hire, in place of his brother, Earl Egerton of Tatton resigned, it is believed the imposing function of in- stallation will take place ia Chester on or about the 17th or 18th of December FARM FIRE AT LITTLE LEIGH.

On Monday night about 10 20 a fire was dis- covered to be raging in the stackyard of Mr. Reuben Fowles, Dawsley heath Farm, and before it WtitS subdued two corn stacks valued at £5OO were damaged to the extent of £250. The origin of the fire is not known. It is said that the whole is covered by insurance.
FIRM AT RUNCORN LAY-BY.

Shortly after ten o'clock, on Monday night, as Constable S Rowlands was patrolling Westfi-ld-road, he observed what appeared to be a conflagration raging near the Runcorn Lay-by. Subsequent investigation proved that a quantity of old sleepers had got on fire through being put in too close proximity to an old rubbish heap which had been set on fire. When Rowlands got to the scene of the fire be found Constable Moores and other men busy extinguishing it. He rendered assistance, and in the end the fire was put out before lOs worth of damage had been done.
NEW JUDGE FOR RUNCORN.

We learn that Mr. Bowen Rowlands, QC, whose appointment as Lounty Court Judge, in succession to Judge Lushington, resigned, was aunonnced on Saturday, has been appointed to the No. 7 circuit as from the 26th instant. No. 7 circuit embraces Bir- kenhead, Northwich, Warrington, Runcorn, etc. and is now presided over by Judge Gwynne James, whom it will be remembered succeeded Judge Ffoulkes.—The Runcorn County Court is fixed for the 29th inst., and will consequently be the :first at which his Honour Judge Rowlands will preside ; and., doubtless, the solicitors of the district will ex- tend to him a bean), welcome.
OmNIIIIAL-BOOTH AT RUNCGUN.

The venerable leader of the salvation Army, General Booth, on Tuesday last, paid Runcorn a visit, with the object of reinstating the cause, and preached to large congregations in the Citadel, High-street, in the afternoon and evening. The Gentral was accompanied by Colonenawley, travel- ling secretary, and known as the Army "Sankey "; Colonel Eadie, the field-secretary; Colonel Roth- well; Major Cox, Major Greenwood, and many others. l n the afternoon General Booth took for his text the 2nd Verse of the 1100th Psalm," Serve the Lord with gladness," and argued strongly in favour(of,the " Joyful religion of the salvationist," whilst at ,night, the 26th verse of the 16th chapter of Matthew, "For what does a man profit if he shall gain the whole world and lose ,his own soul," was the text. Colonel Lawley led the singing, and on the whole very successful meetings were held. During the day General Booth was the guest of Mr R H Posnett.

div.head: SUDDEN DEANE' OF A CHELD AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SUDDEN DEANE' OF A CHELD AT RUNCORN.

At the Runcorn Police Court on Saturday after- noon Mr Robert Dobson, district coroner, held an inquest on the body of Clara Taylor, aged four years. who died suddenly the same morning at 3, Thomas-street., Runcorn. Mr Robert Wright was foreman of the jury.—Mary Elizabeth Earlam, wife of Charles Henry Earlam,engine cleaner,3, Thomas- street, stated that she was not related to the de- ceased at all. The deceased was brought to her house by her request on Thursday, the Bth inst. Witness and her sister brought her from the Work- house. The child slept by the side of witness on Friday night,and she beard nothing of her until five minutes past six that (Saturday) morning. She moved and disturbed witness with a slight cough. Witness got out of bed, and the child appeared as though she would be sick. Witness roused hers husband, and told him to fetch some brandy, and call up Mrs Austin, the next-door neighbour. The child expired immediately afterwards. -The Coroner remarked that Dr McDougall had told him that his opinion was that death was due to convulsions.— The jury returned a verdict that the child died from con vulk ions.

div.head: WARRINGTON
div.p: WARRINGTON

Appointment of Borough Electrical Engineer A special meeting of the Electric Lighting Com- mittee of the Corporation was held at the Town Hall on Monday afternoon, Alderman Monks in the chair, for the purpose of appointing an electrical engineer, to take charge of the electric generating station at Howley. There were originally 65 appli- cants for the position, but the number was reduced to three, and these—Mr. C. R Brown, of Belfast; Mr E. M. Hollingsworth, of St. Helens; and Mr. W. B. Grimsdale—appeared before the committee on Monday. Mr. Grimsdale, who has been super- intending the erection of the generating station, was unanimously selected, and the appoint- ment will date from the Ist December. The salary is £250 per annum, and Mr. Grimsdale has to de- vote the whole of his time to the duties of the office.

Funeral of the late Mrs. Hall. The funeral of the late Mrs Hall, of Hopefield, Lymm (formerly of Bewasy Bridge, Warrington), took place in St. Paul's Churchyard, on Saturday. The chief mourners were :—First coach, Mr Charles Burgess (Warrington), Mr John Jackson (Maccle- field), Mr Charles Woolacott (Manchester), and Mr gdward Coates (Warrington) ; second coach, Mr Arthur Jackson (Blackburn), Mr Alfred Sims ( War- rington), Mr Henry Woolacott (Manchester), and Master Sydney Burgess (Warrington), The cortege left Lymm at two o'clock and arrived at St. Paul's Church at 3.15, where it was met by the Rev. E. R, Tarbuck. vicar, who officiated. There were many floral tokens from various members of the family. The funeral arrangements were carried out by Mr A B Ferries, of the Cross, Lymm.

div.head: Personal.
div.p: Personal.

The Rector of Lymm (ttev. G. B, Thurston), was able to assist at the service on Sunday. The rev. gentleman has been suffering from an attack of in- fluenza, but is now regaining his normal strength and good health.

- On Thursday morning there was a epecial meeting of the Runcorn Urban District Council, heid at the Town Hall, under the presidency of Mr W Handley, J.P., for th 3 purpose of deciding whether £lO,OOO or £5,000 should be invested in the Transporter Bridge under- taking. There were also preeent :—Messrs S Taylor, J Pritchard, E Imison, F Wiswalla W Lightburn, '1 Dean, E Gatley, D Bisbrown, M J Sweetman, H G time, 'l' Jones, J H Salkeld, It H Posnett, J Wilson, eie.,rge Hewitt, with E Marshall (secretary), F A Lake Oa w clerk), and James Wilding (surveyor). The Chairman said as all were aware of the bueieess that had called them together, the best course tier him to follow would bet read the terms of the resolution , passed on the 18th of October last, wheu it was decided to invest £5,000 in the undertaking. having done se he explaieed that the resolution be now propeesd was i to substitute the words " £lO,OOO " for the words I " £5,000 " in the orginal resolution. Mr Imison asked, before the resolution was seconded , whether some means could not he devised for the oise cussion of the subject in private, so that whatever was said nothing weuld be done that might prevent investors tram putting their meney in it. Mr. S. Taylor objected to any such course as the Council going into Committee over the affair. I The Cnairman observed that Mr. Imison had not 'etc- posed that the Council go int.) Committee. He only asked whether something could not be devised that would make it possible to privately discuss its financial aspect. Mr. Imison said that was so, and his only reason for so doileg, was that the subject could be fully discussed, and all would be free to make use of any information tney might possess, without at the same time doing any- thing that would tend to injure the undertaking. Mr Taylor, however, still objected to the course pro- posed by Mr Imieon, and did not see what harm could come from the fullest publicity. ' Mr J Wilson then seconded the proposition put from the chair, that the £lO,OOO be investeci, anei reserved the right of addressing the Council later. Mr Grice proposed as an amendment that the £5,000 be invested as originally agreed, with or without a .d,rector. He was in no way antagonistic to the bridge, and indeed thought it would be a good thing for the town, and a good thing for the investors. That was only a matter of opinion without going into the merits or demerits of the scheme. He c.intendeo that the Council had always been in the past very anxious to keep down the rates and couid not afford the expenditure. Mr. J W Ligiatburn seeended the amendment, and, in furtheranee'ot the faith that was in him, said he did not thick it was worth the additional £5,000 to have a ciiree• tor. Again, it they had a director, one in nine could not get the other eight to agree to run a night-car when the eight were convinced that to do so would not be a commercial success. They also lost sight of the fact that they already had a director on the beard in the person of Sir J T Brunner. He did not think there was a single person who would deny that Sir J T Brunner had worked for the interests of the town in a most praiseworthy manner in the past, and he felt that they had in him still a gentleman who would interest himself in their behalf. Again, replying to some of his critics, he would urge that it was not a question of logic, but a question of risk, that he had to ar.swer, and he thought it better to risk the smaller amount. With regard to the ratepayers' meeting, tha' had been held, he wished to point out that it was for the purpose of cue am n members of the Council having an opportuhity of conferring with the ratepayers. The Council did not pledge themselves to accept the dictum of that meeting. Drawing a comparison with Widnes, it was agreed that Widnes should invest £25,000, and same would illustrate that Runcoru's £5,000 in comparison was but a paltry matter. He differed, it was not so paltry as they would make out. I.d. in the £ for Widnes produced some £6OO, ishil9t a lde in the £ for Runcorn only produced some £2OO, so that really speaking Runcorn's ratio to Widne.s would be one-third, or £B,OOO. Thus, £5,000 was not so paltry as it would appear at first sight. Mr. Salketd's reasons for supporting Mr Grice's amend ment were threefold. First : He did not think that Runcorn in its present state could afford £lO,OOO. A 33 6.1 rate for next year was more or less indicated. Trade was not brisk .; and it meant a possible increase of 5,1 in the £on the rates. Secondly, the Transporter Bridge was somewhat of a specu'ation. and the invest- ment of public funds was a risk, especially where deben- ture or other shares were likely to be issued. He thought the interests of the communities of Widnes and Runcorn could well be left in the hands of such gentlemen as the promoters were. Mr D I3isbrown supported the resolution. As a town Runcorn was isolated, and it was high time that they had another means of communication with the cuter world. The only point of difference between them seemed to be £5,000 or £lO,OOO. He did not maintain that it was absolutely necessary to have a director, but tey had virtually, by the original resolution, estab- nehed the tact that they would be justified in investing £5,000 if they got a directorship with it. So long then as they could obtain a director for an extra £5,000 it would be of great advantage to have someone to repre- sent them. Widnes by their attitude secured two direc- tors, and it would be unfair if Runcorn were without. Referrine to the remissness of the old Board of Commis- sioners 30 years ago, Mr Bisbrown added, that if they , failed to use the opportunity of securing a directorship, they %you'd in years to come be derided for their short- , bighted policy. Mr T Dean also supported the resolution on the grounds of the benefits that would accrue to the towns- people from tbe fact that the London and North- Western Railway Company's bridge would have to reduce its fares to compete with it, also, he said, he was obliged to take cognisance of the fact that the Council had consulted the ratepayers and got an expression of opinion from them, which although some members might pooh! poohl he was obliged to respect. Mr Lightburne No. We do not pooh I pooh I (Laughter.) Mr Dean, continuing, considered the extra speculation well worth a director. Mr Imison asked for information in the matter of the meeting alluded to, and that the advertisement calling it be read. This the Chairman did, when it was shown to be addressed to the ratepayers. Mr. Wiswall supported the amendment on the principle of choosing the lesser evil. He did not think that the Transperter Bridge was going to be what it was " cracked cut" to be. It was also evident that the London and North-Western Railway Compeny did net fear its opposition as was illustrated by the way they very reedits agreed to its adoptions. He would like to put it to the supporters, and to the promoters of the bridge, too, that the cost of the undertaking will be £120,000. Mr Wood, the engineer, in that very room had said that the bridge would have to he doubled, which meant that at some future date the Council would be called upon to invest another £lO,OOO.

Mr. Poenett : No. Mr. Wiswall : Mr.Posnett wants to put it differently. but it doesn't follow that because it is doublfd it will pay. Thus they could eel it would cost £240,000 to make the bridge really effective and attain its object. The exit of a permanent bridge had been stated by no less an authority than Sir Douglas Fox, to be £200,000, Indeed, the C,)unty Council thought they might put more on. He would put it to the promoters, whether it would not be worth while to re-consider the Bridge scheme, and go in for a permanent bridge, which would really cost less, and to it attach the same tolls. If the Council did decide to invest £IO,OOO in this concern, he only hoped the Local Government Board would hold an inquiry,and refuse to sanction such a foolish procedure, Mr. Imison said Mr. Wiswall's speech exactly illustra- ted why he wished the discussion in committee. The question the Council had to decide was whether the representation they would secure was worth £lO,OOO. He asked that Mr. Lake's letter to the promoters should be read.

Mr. Lake read the letter which Rot forth that the Council had a special right to consideration because they had rendered the promoters every assistance in their power in passing the Bill, and because of their interest in the approaches to the proposed bridge. and expressing the hone that the promoters would grant a director for £5,000.—1n reply the promoters regretted they could not alter their decision.

Mr. Imison (continuing), said the promoters had treated the Council unhandsomely, and, for that reason he suggested invoking the aid of Sir John Brunner. In this matter Sir John's services would be peculiarly vlivable. The Council had frequently approached him upon far less important matters than this, and he might succeed where the Council had failed The Company proposed to raise £33,000 by borrowing, and when those norrowing powers were exhausted it would be necessary for the Company either to issue de benture stock, which would depreciate the value of the Councils Security, or they would have to go into volun- tary liquidation for the purpose of issuirg flesh shares.' The Council would be obliged to contribute fresh c..pi- tal in order to save the capital they had already invested As to the rate at which the Council could borrow the money to insest, Mr Imison pointed out that authori- ties with unrivalled ere dit could not borrow at a less rate than 31 per cent for 30 years, and at that rate the repayment would require £560 per year from the rates. The figures laid before the Council and the public were simply estimates. The Company had not received a single t( nder for the 9 ork proposed to be carried out ; and it wat not unreasonable to suppose the estimates would Le largely exceed, ol aed they ought to stipulate the hours the bridge v. 1.. e..• werking day and night. If Mr. Bisbrown, consisttu, e r,, •,•;s'• as be was, would propose to spend £srlo a ) ear up ehrspitsl, the Council could do their duty and ttie hi&pal could to opened the year round, for the use of the general pub ic and probably many lives would be saved. div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT
COUNCIL.

Mr. Jams Knowles J.P., preilded over the fortnightly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, and there were present :—Messrs S Woodward, J Mclntyre. T Darlington, J Mounfield, T Lewis, T Baxter C.C., T Wright, H Mawdsley, J Spruce, C Roylance, P Gleave, J Bolshow, J W Baguley, E Turner, Horton,E Brethertoti, J M Williams, P Leather. G F Ashton (clerk) W E Hough (assistant clerk),Dr Adams(medical officer),J Far- rington (inspector), and Diggle and Swinton (surveyors).
HELSEY WATERWORKS.

Helsby Parochial Committee submitted a recommenda- tion to ask the lielsby and District Waterworks Com- pany upon what terms they wou!d sell their undertaking and at the same time to disclose their agreement with the Telegraph Company.—Passed on the motion of Mr. Williams.
WESTON AND RUNCORN ROAD.

Under the heading" Proposed new Main-road" dated November Bth, Mr R Potts clerk to the Cheshire County Council stated "Adverting to your letter of the 20th Sep- tember last, my Committee has postponed the consider- ation of the application menttoned therein to next year and has appointed a sub-committee to inspect the high- ways and to reeport thereon. The committee dealt in a similar manner with an application from the Runcorn Urban District Council to have the highway between Runcorn railway station and Weston township declared a main-road."
RUNCORN TANNERIES AND RIVERS POLLUTION.

The Clerk submitted correspondence with the Cheshire County Council in respect to rivers pollution especially dealing with the tanneries in Runcorn district. The County Medical Officer, Dr Vacher. had visited the tanneries of the Elighfield Tannery Company, Messrs John Ockleston and Son, and Messrs Pierpoint, and reported that these firms were doing all they could to promote the making of a sewer by the Runcsrn Rare! District Council, which would receive the efflaents from the tanneries and the estimated cost was £1,200. The three firms thought it wmuld be reasonable to be charged one third of this sum, provided an agree- ment were come to that the tanneries should have the convenience of discharging their effluents into the sewer. Dr Vacher visited Messrs Reynolds tannery upon a later date and reported that it appeared to be conducted on similar lines to the Runcorn tanneries. The effluent flow- ing into the Ship Canal was decidedly worse tban the Effluent in February last. The County Council intimated to the Rural Council that they must take action with- out delay to put a stop to the pollution of the streams within their district, avid expressed the opinion of the Rivers Pollution Committee that they should do all they possibly could to protect the tanneries carrying on business in the district.
The Clerk .poioted out that tbe only tannery in the rural district was Messrs. Reynolds ; the others being in the urban district of Runcorn.

The County Medical Officer's report on Reynolds' tannery was referred to Dr Adams. The Clerk said there were a number of streams re- ferred to. In regard to Halton Brook the Halton Com- mittee had the question under consideration. They wanted if possible to devise a scheme similar to the one proposed for Hatton, but they were unable to deal with the matter until they saw whether the Local Govern- ment Board would accept the Elatton Scheme. In the case of the pollution of two streams at flashy, Helsby Committee were getting out an expensive sewerage scheme as quickly as they cou!d. Helsby Committee were now advertising their intention to take land out- side their district, and as three months' notice bad to be given, they could not move until the expiration of that time.

Mr. Woodward said the Council were moving as fast as it was desirable for them to do,and the County Coun- cil had no right to ush them. The Clerk was instructed to write to that effect. NEW BYE-LAWS FOR STOCKTON HEATH.

The Clerk submitted copies of byelaws made by the District Council with respect to water closets, earth- closets, privies, ashrits and cesspools in connection with buildings in tbe parish of Stockton Heath. _ _
The ceal of the Council was affixed. THE THELWALL NUISANCE.

Me3srs Long and Son of Grappenhall, wrote as follows under date, November 10th. "Mr Farrington conveyed to us on the 7th inst the wish of your Board that the length of the Brook in Waste-lane in this township con- veying our effluent to the culvert under the Manchester Ship Canal (Bridgewater) should be cleaned out, and we beg to notify you that this was effectively done on the Bth inst."

Out of a large numbr,r of applich,nts, Antwis3 of King sley was appointed driver of the steam road roller. This was all the business of public interest.
Crosfield Ambulance Challenge Shield.

The annual competition for the Crosfield Chal- lenge Shield, t-ok place at the Gymnasium on Saturday afternoon. The competing teams were Blackpool, Accrington, Kendal, Edentield. and War- rington. The judges were (theory) Dr. Thompson, of Oldham, and for the drill and stretcher work District Secretary, A. L. Garnett, of Burnley. The contest vas very keen, Blackpool and Accrington tying. These teavas were tested a second time theoretically by Dr. Thompson, which resulted in Blackpool obtaining the shield. Amongst those present were Deput3 -Commissioner Lieutenant Colonel Trimble, of Preston, Dr. Reginald Smith ,and the Rev. A.S. Cameron. After the competition a very substantial tea was provided at the Patten Arms I Hotel by Mr. Arthur Crosfield, after which an enjoyable smoker was held. The party broke up about 9 o'clock, on account of the visitors having to catch their various trains home. A vote of thanks was passed to the judges for the valuable services rendered by them.

Choir Festival at Bold-street Wesleyan Church. Toe creditable efficiency to which the choir of Bold- street Wesleyan Church has attained, was demonstrated on Sunday and Monday when the annual festival took place. There were three services on Sunday, at 10.30, 3 o'clock and 6.30, and they were all largely attended. At the morning service the Rev T Bishop preached a sermon appropriate for the occasion on "The New song." The musical portion of the service had been caretully arranged and the choir and other vocal- ists serd instrumentalists who took part acquitted them- selves most admirably. Mr Frank Hickman presided at the organ and gave a fine exposition of his power over the" king of instruments." The wed-balanced choir gave a capital interpretation of the anthem "Send . out Thy lieht and Thy truth",(Gounod) and also creditably sang Spobr's "Sanctus," Mr S H Oilier teking the solo passages. Miss Dora Gilpin, A.R.C.M., of West Bromwich, Birmingham, is the possessor of a rich soprano voice, and she was heard to great advan- tage in the trying solo " From Mighty Kings" (Judas Maccabmus.)—ln the afternoon a musical service was held, :qr. 11. G. Henshall presiding.—The Chairman, in his opening remarks, expressed bis opinioa thee the great need of the church was a brighter and more musical service. Mr. W. 11, Payton, the able organist at Wycliffe Church, was at the organ, and won high encomiums for the skilful manner in which he played " Fantasia in E " (lissse), Smart'e "Andante in Fe' " Toccato in G" (Dubois). " Traumerei " (Schumann), and "Triumphal March ". (Lemmens.) Mr. R. H. Pearson contributed a couple of violin solos "Canzona" (Bohm), and "Cava- tina " (Adlemao), in both of which he displayed his cus- tomary ability. Miss Gilpin and Mr. A. Griffiths delighted the congregation with their rendition of "Love divine," and Miss Gilpin effectively sang.Gouned's " Divine Redeemer "—At the evening service the Rev. H., G. Roberts preached on "The ministry of music.' The choir sang " I waited for the Lord." (Mendelssohn), Miss Gilpiu and Mrs. Dobson ren- dering the solos in a pleasing manner. Mr. A. Griffiths was in capital voice and did ample justice to "Glory to Thee" (Gohnod). Mr Hickman played "Offer- toire in F Mieor " (Salo no) and "Ss Ann's Fugue" (Bach). Collections were taken at each service in aid of the choir funds.—On Monday evening, Mr R A Nay lo' presided over the proceedings, when Mauncier's sacred cantata "Penitence, Pardo') and Peace" was ren- dered by the choir under the conductorship of Mr W Payton. The excellent singing showed that much time must have been devoted to training the choir, and the cantata received capital treatment at their hands. The soloists were Miss Dora Gilpin, Mr Arthur Griffiths, and Mr W H Wallington. Miss Gilpin, it was stated was suffering from a coil, but nevertheless, este sang most effectively. Her best effort was Liddle's " Abide with me" which she rendered very expressively, and was obliged to comply with the demand of the audience for repetition. Mr. Hickman accompanied on the organ and also played the Organ Sonata No. 111 (Mendelssobn) with much taste.—During an interval the Chairman made a few remarks. He said he felt sure he was voic- ing their sentiments when he said that Mr Payton, Mr Hickman, and all associated with them in the performs ance that evening were to be highly complimented upon the admirable manner in which they hid produced that cantata. He had been asked to apologize to them on behalf of Miss Gilpin and Mr Wallnieton because they had had colds, but he was of the opinion that if he had not made the intimation to the eudisnce, they would not have found it out, because the Ringing had been of a high class character. They met together for the pur- pose of offering little praise—it was not much for them to offer—to the Great Creator of the Universe, for He deserved all the praise not only for His creation but for His preservation, and it was something to be proud of that they, as children of one common Father— the Lord God Omnipotent—were permitted with their feeble voices to sine. His presise that day. He had read a little sentence written by some great man to the effect that no one who did no: praise would find a heavereeither in this world or the wurld to Come. They believed that in the glorious future, to which they were looking forward, there would be one great and loud anthem of praise throughout all eternity. And it seemed to him to he something to illuminate the present life—with all its troubles, trials, and disappointments— to know that if they had performed their mission here, served their Maker faithfully and offered Him the praise of their feeble lips,thet there was the proud future tefore them to look forward to, when they could sing in nobler songs of tribute to the Almighty, to the King of Kings and the Lord of Lords. (Hear, hear.) It was a great pleasure to him to attend that meeting for the purpose of supporting Mr•Hickman.the orgenist,and he rejoiced with him upon the :success of his endeavours and those who had been pleased to give their services. (Applause,) Mr R G Hensball proposed a vote of thanks to Mr Naylor and to those who had given their services On Sunday and that evening,especially to the organist. The trustees made a good choice when they appointed Mr Hickman some months ago to the post of organist. The choir festival marked a red-letter day in the history of the Church, and he hoped it would be an omen of what was to come in the future.—The Rev T Bishop seconded, and the motion was carried.—The Rev T Bishop announced that the collections taken at the Sunday ser- vices and that evening amounted to £42 49 6d. (Applause.)

OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. Mr. Whetnall presided at the meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society on Sunday afternoon. In the course of a brief address, he spoke on hereditc.ry drunkenness, and showed that the hatitsuf drunkarth were transmitted to their children. Be urged that it only for the children's sake, they ought to Co all in their power to combat the terrible ravages of strong drink.—Mr. wbitesido, of Manchester, delivered a thoughtful address on service for Jesus Christ, in which ho showed the calls and demands of that service, and the reward which was received for faithful service. The meeting was also taken part in by the Rev. Jol'n Yonge, Mr. Cotton, Mr. T. Hawthorn and Mr. B. Farrar.

LANCASHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.
Warrington Surprised at Barrow.

Following a period of in-ctivity, which was only re- lieved by a noople of inconsequential " friendlies." Barrow on Saturday once more resumed their resoon- sibility in the Senior Competition. They e Itertainel Warrington at Cavendish Park in a mann-.!r such as gave just cause for rejoicing among their followers Since their admission into tne charmed circle they had never given so attractive a display of clever -foot. ball as they did on Saturday against the visitors from Warrington. Both teams were at full ,t,ength. From the commeneerrent of operations the Shipbuilders begao in a businesslike and methodical fashion, but their at- pirations to victory rec,iced a rude shoch in the early moments of the game through the nimbler) -ss of F sh, who carved out a passage arnlng his opp infers in noes - artistic style. But B owker soon put his side on level terms by scoring an equaly meritorious try*, whici.., like Fish, he failed to improve. The conest contimi,d to be keenlr played, and the total absstnce of any semb- lance of too robust play made the ram all the more enjoyable. Fat an iufringement Bat:ow cooceded a hrece of points to Warrington, and placel themselves in a minority of two Hughes got clear of all 0)0 S i i hut the übiquitous Fish grabbed him from b-hind. How- ever, the effort led up to) some eke passing across the ground to Bamberg and altheugh little he put suffic:en7 dash into his run to carry him over the line, and tros minority of two became a majority 4 one. Theo the onlookers had a little morn of Fkli, who ran and dodgeo with Comparative ease to the other wing, and doubling back gave the bail to Dickenson' who made a bungle of it. The attempts to tackle Fish were at times u liempus. Through the instrumentality of Wharton and Platt, play went back to the other ane, where fickle and then Bowker gat clear, and the final pass to Bowden resulted in a capital try. At half-time Barrow were in the satis- factory position of leading by four poirta. The best effort of the afternoon's play came from the home who in the second half nombiord so fft-cti .ely that Warrington's defence e mold not prevent Bowden from scoring his second try und,r the posts, hut Proci-or, usually so ' safb at short kicks at goal, made a very indifferenfattsmpt to add two points. Rigiot up to no- side Barrow were distinctly the better team, and rely resolute Tacklino kept the score from increasing,, except a dropped goal by Boseker.

div.head: NOTES.

_NEGLIGENT FATHER SENT T PBISON —Joseph Lancaster was charged with running away from the Borough on the 13th August. leaving his five children chargeable to the Union.--Mr, B. Shearer prosecuted on behalf of the Guar- dians. and stated that the prisoner together with a woman to whom it was thought he was married, en n the children came to Warrington early in the year. He was employed by the Warrington Carriage Co., but he left the Borough, and the woman and children were admitted to the Workhouse. They had cost the Guardians nearly £3O. It had since transpired that the prisoner was not married to the woman and three of the children were his late wife's.—lnspector Hackett informed the magistrates that the family had been under the observation of the N.S.P.C.C., in the Macciesfitid district. It was the intention of the society to take legal proceedings, but the family absconded to Warrington. After some difficulty he traced them to Lyons-street. and he found the house to be fairly clean. The I+edding on which the children slept consisted of two bags of flocks covered with rage, and thE baby was in a very emulator' condition. The children appeared to be much neglected .—Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month with hard labour.

div.head: DRUNKEN SAILORS It POLICE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: DRUNKEN SAILORS It POLICE AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessiona on Monday before Messrs. Reynolds and W Handley, John Johnson, a Swede, and Neil Neilson, a Dane, both seamen on the timber ship Mareni moored at the lay-by, were charged with being drunk and disorderly on Sunday night. Neilson was also charged with assaulting Detective Sergeant Gregory. The evidence showed that at 10-15 on Sunday night Detective Gregory in plain clothes, and Constable' Wilding and Shaw were on duty in Devonshire-square, when they saw the prisoners and three other sailers come up Regent-street. All were drunk and noisy and Johnson was walking in his stockinged feet and was whirling his shoes round his head. Neilson was using most filthy language. Gregory informed him he was a policeman and told him to go quietly to his ship where- upon Neilson struck him on the face with his fist, kicked him and threatened that had be a knife he would send it through his heart. Gregory closed with Neilson and both went to the ground. Johnson and another sailor interfered and Shaw arrested Johnson and Wilding the other man. Gregory mastered his assailant and handcaffed him. When Wilding hid reached Opp- site Dr Dr McDougall's with his capture,two sailors set up- on him,tripped him down,and all three made off. Wild- ing went in pursuit, when a dog flew at him and bit him on the leg.—Mr Handley observed that these men must have been made mad with drink somewlaere.—Soperin- tendent Pearson said the police had an Herr where they had been and there mioht be a sequel to this case. Each prisoner was fined 5s and costs 7s for being drunk and Neilson was fined 103 and costs 7s for the assault

On Tuesday Gustaf Colcen, Olaf Golsen, and Ariel Johanafen, the other seamen referred to in the above case, were brought up charged resnectively with being drunk and disorderly, and assaulting Gmstable Wilding iu the execution of his duty. The evidence was the same as in the previous case, but it was shown that Olaf Calsen, had given the c•.ri -t 01, a. " Jhuck in the neck "and a severe kick.—Mr. F. J. Norman, who pre- sided, characterised Olars offence as a very serious one and fined him £1 and 10. costs or 21 days; the other Colson was fined 5s and-63. costs, or seven diyg, and Jobanafen, 10s. and 10s. costs or seven days.
