RUGBY FOOTBALL.

eon and Jones took advantage of he mistake to kick over the line and. Meisenger dashed up and dropped upon the ball. Farmer failed to add the goal points. By kicking and good following up by the forwards Wigan paid a visit to the Runcorn end, but a splendid passing run by Jolley, Faulkner and Richardson trans- ferred play to Wigan quarters, where Middleton and Eckersley drove them back. At centre Jolley and Faulkner exchanged and the latter after cleverly beat- ing a Couple of men, pirted,Zo C. Butterworth who ran well arid evading Andertots, snmed bebind the posts. Again Farmer :ailed to kick a goal. Wi ;an now strove hard to male h adway but were well field, and the Runcorn forwards took play to Wigan line where Jolley scored, Houghton failing at goal. Goaded by these reverses, the visitors played with desperate energy and a combined movement by the forwards took play to the Runcorn hue, where scrummage succeeded scrummage and at . length Rigby forced himself over and scored. Ton same, player kicked a goal. Ends were changed with Ruucorn leading by nine paints to three. Runcorn mtarted and at once pressed, and Mebsenger scored a try in smart style Jolley kicking a goal. Tee home team were now demonstrating their fuperiority in all departments of the game. By clever passing and running Wigan were kept on the defensive and tries came in rapid succession. Messenger scored his third try as a result of combined passing, sue then Jo:ley dropped a goal. Again Messenger put the final touch to a smart passing bout in which Jolley, Faulkner, and Richardson were the chief executors but this time, Jolley faiied to add the goal points. Wigan were now thoroughly disheartened and Richardson and Fathlkner each. ran in ,martves and Jolley converted both. Runcorn thus woe in ridiculous ease by 5 goals 8 tried, 34 points to Wigan 1 coal 1 try, 5 points.

whole of the game, ran oil% winners by tree goals to two. The tie tvas taken In hand by a first-class Were° n Mr. Scragg of Crewe, who always had the players well in hand. The visitors won the toss and naturally took advantage of the wind and hill. Linton starting on behalf of Earlestown before about 500 spectators. Tao opening exchanges were all in tavour of Nantwinh who took full advantage of the strong wind and tnade matters:warm for the home defenders. Twenty-five minutes had gone by when Mort met the ball from Heyes's return and banged it past Chew thus scoring the first goal for Nantwich. Earlestown seemed utterly unable to do anything:right and as a result they gave the visitors' custodian very little trouble. What shots he had to deal with he negotiated in masterly style and the inter- val therefore came with Nantwich still leading by one to nil. The second half had only just re-started when Settle put the teams on an equality but immedi- ately afterwards Rhoadan again gave the visitors the lead and soon supplemented this with a third, Chew having no chance with eitheg of the shots which beat him. With the homestersitwo goals in arrears matters seemed hopeless from an Earlestown supporter's point of view, for although they did most of the pressing they could only score once, Bartley, placing the leather in the net from a scrimmage. The game had hardly been vi-.tarted before the whistle blew for the cessation, with the visitors victorious by three goals to two. The least said about the display of the homesters, the better. Their supporters were simply disgusted with them and they had good reasen to be. Coming as it did on top of the grand display against Blackburn Rovers Reserve, it is harder to understand than ever. The visitors who were only lads were a smart lot never— theless, and played a clean business-like game through- out.
Warrington Cup, First Round.
Warrington St. Mary's v. Warrington Trinity.

Played on Saturday at Howley. The visitors started with ten men.. The opening stages were greatly in favour of Trinity, the home custodian being -several times called upon to save. Thompson relieved with a huge kick, to which Stockton only weakly responded. Robin- son gained possession, and made a fine run, Bradshaw' (who had just arrived) clearing in the nick of time. '[he home forwards often got going, but Murray, who was playing a sterling game, always proved a stumbling block. Trinity were several times penalised in front of ' goal, but Parry managed to keep his charge clear. At the interval there was no score. On resuming, the Saints went away with a rush. but Murray was safe. A fine passing movement by Lavell, Stockton, and Baker ended in the latter striking the uprights. A free kick against the visitors was headed .out by Bradshaw. Robinson got posstssion, and passed to Meachiu, and that player cleverly mataceuvred the leather past Parry.. For the next ten ' minutes the Saints were penned in their own goal. Hennigan headed out a dangerous shot, and Meachin getting the ball at his toes ran thme parts the length of the field and scored, the shot knocking Parry through his own goal. Final: • Warrington St. Mary's, two goals; Warringted Trinity, nil.

div.head: AFTER THE WAR.
div.p: AFTER THE WAR.
The Prospects of South Africa.

In the November issue of FEILDEN'S MAGAZINH there is an editorial review of the prospects of South Africa within the near future, and of the opportunities for its unhampered development now that the incubus of Boer rule is removed from what by a misnomer was called the South African "Republics." and freedom under a just and bones t government is to be the lot of its inhabitants in every portion of tue country. After giving a concise statistical summary of the progress of the gold mining iedustry since 1887, very largely due to the energy and eitterprise of the hated " Outlanders," who, though said to be unwelcome to tile " simple . and pastoral " Boers, erere not only encouraged but directly invited by Presi- dent Kruger, who took good care to obtain a respect- able share of the wealth derived by r heir industry from the auriferous soil, the writer points out that cold min- ing is not the °ley impirtant induetry in South Africa when has derived benefit frills enterprising capitalists, i e., from the class of men who often have been called the curse of South Africa. Net only railway Wilding and. electrical engineering was developed by means of the money they invested, but ever agricultural enter- prise was fostered by them te a cot.siderible extent, to- warrior witlithe establishment of important collieries. " Taking one case as an illu,trition," says the writer of the article," we may refer to the extensive series of industrial ventures cemmenced a year or two agi by the Vereeniging EstatEs, Limited. a:: Vereenigiog and Vilj ion's Drift. In addition to two collieries, one on eien side of the Vaal River, and constituting one of the largest coal-mining schemes in South Atrica, there are, or were,a large and well-equipped brick end tile factory, an extensive grain-growing and general agricultural undertaking with a complete milling lant, and a large ' stock-hreediog establishment. The E•tates inOtude some 22 farms, covering over 130,000 acres. A portion of the property is within the Veal River Colony. The agricultural estate was equipped with the most modern steam ploughs, threshers, winnowers. and other mechinerY for the cultivation of 15,000 acres reclaimed from the bare veldt. About 600 acres on the south bank of the river were under irrigation, a system which was being largely extended at the outbreak of the recent rebellion. In the forestry rection there are some 600,000 oak trees, some of these being 20ft. high at aim age of a little mortfethen lour years. Altogether 3 million trees are included in this departmentee large number being pines of varioui kards. The stock-breening establishment was devoted largely to mulee although cattle-raising and horse-breeding has not beers overlooked. Fruit-growing is also likely to become a feature of the estatieand a number of orchards have :already been planted. As the line, formerly known as the Orange Free State Railway, depends entirely on the collieries of the estate for fueeit is only natural that the coal-mining department ehould form a most valu- able pert of the Company's operations. In .addi- ttoo, we believe that the Cape Government Railway and the De Beers . Company are also large i buyers. Coal mining is =ducted at two points, each connected with the railway system." As a specimen of ' enterprise in another direction the author %Igo mentions tho establishment of the Band Central Electric Works at Brakpen by two English cspitali3ts, by whom the contract for the whole-plant was awarded to Messrs. Siemens & Ha'ske, who equipped the works with boilers of the Sr emnriillor multitunular type and enemas of tee Saechsieche Meschinen Fabrik, while the dynamee and electrical appliances were of their own maks. Alluding to these facts, and in agreement with the main principle adopted by " Fielden'a Maisszine." the writer in the I foliowing.words urges British engineers to avail them- selves of the opportunities now open to them, and not, as heretofore, leave industriel engineering enter- prise too much in the hands of foreigners : " Gee of the least satisfactory circumstance's .crinnected with this and other enterprises in South Africa is the fact that foreign firms have been too much in evidence to please those who have the interests of British inchis- tries at heart. Probably other nation,. have been unduly favoured in the past.but there are evidences that a good deal of their success is to be attributed to greater activity and superior commercial organisation. . . Already we hear that foreign firms are on the alert, and are.prepering to meet the expected demand ; but very 'little evidence is ferthcomine to show that BritWr firms have yet nnoreciated the nos-Noe. Freedom hi s now come Cm South Africa, and no one doubts that all the c ilsinies, old and eew, are about to enter, thnush per- haps no: Immediately, upon a time of uriparellel-d pros- perity and proerees, in which it is our hope that the mother coontre may fully participate."

div.head: Recreation.
div.p: Recreation.

Sir,—l was pleasd to see in th " Evaminer "of the 17th inst. that two of our Town Ceuncillors had be-n addressing a meeting of the P.S. A. Mr. Bt.,anett ap- peared to want a test applied to Warrington, but if our Lord Jesus Christ caolf, to Warrington as 'a property- owner, and went into the streets referred to he would not attend on rent day unless it was to inform the tenants that be would not receive any more rents until the houses were put in a proper sanitary condition. I am delighted to hear that thP trustees for Silver- Street Schools are making every preparation for acquir- ing the fifteen houses (forming the block) for school and recreation ground enlargements. I trust the owner of the said proparty mill meet them in a Christian spirit, and, that more roomy schools and healthier children may be the result. Thm there is the oppoaite side of the Street:could nothing be done to improve on the property standing there? There is no gymnasium or baths, or library ; or any other means of recreation in that end of the town, and young people after doing a hard day's work cannot be expected to walk to the other end of the town. Mope we shall hear more from someone who is better able to use the pen than myself. Thanking you in anticipation.—l am yours respect- Lally, A WORKINGMAN.

div.head: Ignorant Runcorn.
div.p: Ignorant Runcorn.
Sir,—lt is a waste of time to correspond with OH9 who has not the candour to admit himself wrong when Clearly proved so.

The Case stands thus : (1). "One of the Ignorant" not daring to sign his own name in de an anonymous attack upon Canon Ma. seemi Wood for saying, as he alleged, at St. Michael's Bazaar, teat the people of Runcorn were poor and ignor- ant.

(2). I replied that I was with Canon Maitland Wood onthe platform at the time, and that he never said any such thing—an i further, I added, that even if he had, inasmuch as the speech was a humorous one in which the Vicar was describing himself and his own friends, it would have been ridiculous to write as "One of the Ignorant" did. (3). In the face of this emphatic denial. "one of the Ignorant" will neither withdraw nor express regret for his cowardly attack on the Vicar. Comment is needless—l confidently leave your readers to draw their own conclusions both about this, and his abaurdly false remarks as to making assertions in public and withdrawing them in private letters.—Yours truly, W. H. STABLES. Runcorn, November 20th, 1900.

div.head: SIR JOHN BRUNNER ON CHARTERED COMPANIES.
div.p: SIR JOHN BRUNNER ON CHARTERED COMPANIES.

On Wednesday night, Sir John Brunner, member for Northwich Division, took part in two meetings to inaugurate a Liberal Association for Biliddlewich, a por- tion of Northwich Division. Alluding to the transactions of the Government with the Royal Niger Company, Sir John said he had regar- ded the original grant of a charter to the Niger Company as a lamentable blunder. Chartered companies always had gone wrong, for they had concerned themselves with their pockets at the expense of the people whom they had been given the power to govern. He was a shareholder in this Royal Niger Company, not for per- eonsl interest, but for the simple purpose of acquiring information. For that purpose also he bad small invest- ments placed in Argentina, in the north of India, and in North America, and consequently he received reports with regard to the trade of those parts of the world which fitted him the better to represent an industrial constituency in Parliament. His investment in the Royal Niger Company was not more, he believed than £2OO or £3OO, but whatever it was he received double the sum when the Government bought him up. (Laughter.) The Company got a charter, misman- aged its affairs brought discredit upon the fair fame of England, and in order to bring this shame that had been oast upon the nation to an end the Government bought the Company up at double the price of the shares. N 3 one who knew the history of the British South Africa Company for the last five or six years could be ign2rant of the enormous discredit and of the terrible dangers which had been brought upon the country by the doings of that Company in South Africa. He promiacd. his constituents as a Liberal member of Perlis rnent that never again, so far as his efforts could prevent it should any part of the world under the British flag be governed otherwise than by the representatives of the Queen and the De ,pie. (Applause.) In his opinion the Government would have to buy up the British South Africa Company at an enormous price, and there was net a man on either front bench in the House of Corn- moons who could not give the soundest and most irrefrag- able and absolutely unanswerable reasons why the Gov- ernment should buy that company up. The question would be how much per share should be paid, and how much profit should be given to the fortunate owners of shares in that company. He would vote that the share- holders should have no more than the fair value of their property, and rather than reward them he would endea- vour to bring it about that they should he punished for their mismanagement of affairs in South Africa. (Applause.) The salt trade of Cheshire was now feeling the effects of the increased duties on salt in Nigeria, but that increase had been made necessary by the wars in which the Royal Niger Company had involved that country. Lot peace, retrenchment, and reform be adopted in Nigeria as they ought to he adopted in this country, and then the salt trade of Cheshire would re- vive. (Applause.)

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS. ---- Mr, Kruger's Arrival.
Speech at Marseilles.
"Fighting a Barbarous Nation." Marseilles, Thursday, 11.30 a.m..—Mr. Kruger landed at 10.45.
MARSEILLES, 11.35 A.M.

On landing at Marseilles ex-Presidentl Kruger made a speech, in which he thanked the French Government for his sympathy with the Transvaal Government and the cardiality of his reception. This remark was, says the Exchange Telegraph Company's correspondent. received with ironical laughter. He went on to remark that since Dr. Jameson endeavoured to conquer the country without making a fight a terrible war had been thrust upon them,'notwithstandingihis reiter- ated claim for arbitration, which had been refused by England. The war was a barbarous one, and the Boers had been fighting a barbarous nation. He said he was profoundly touched by his wel- come to France, which was the home of liberty. Their farms were being burnt, their wives hunted from their homes, whilst their husbands were fighting en the battlefield. But whatever was done, the Boers would resist to the bitter end.
Dr Leyds and Messrs Grobler and Fischer re- mained standing behind the es-Preßident while his speech was being delivered. Mr Kruger then pro- ceeded in a landau to the Hotel Noailles.

div.head: Warrington Volunteers Sent Back to Duty. .•_ _ _
div.p: Warrington Volunteers Sent Back to Duty. .•_ _ _

A letter has been received at St Helens from Sergeant Gardner, of the volunteer contingent of the let South Lancashire Regiment is South Africa. In it Sergeant Gardner states that Lord Roberts dischar.;ed the Volun- teers on October 13th, and they were preparing to embark for home when suddenly notice was received that the Boers w ,re threatening Dundee. The cense- queues was that the men, instead of going home, we-it to a hill ten miles from Dundee, where they were entrenched in expectation of a Boer attick. He adds that the hill is called Gregory's Nek, and that the men are having a good time. Ic is nrobahle, therefore, that the return of the Warrington Volunteers will be delayed The "Welcome Home" to Volunteers

div.head: Benefit Night at the Fair.
div.p: Benefit Night at the Fair.

On Tuesday evening the Fair Ground in Queen-street, was visited by thousands of people, Mr. Wallie, the proprietor of the electric horses, and Mr. Clarke, the proprietor of the einem apt, having agfir agreed to give the proce3ds of the eve. after deduct- ing certain expenses) towards the f or entertaining the Warrington Volunteers on their return home. The Volunteer Band was in attendance at sevee o'clock, and played a selection of music during the evening. His Worship the Mayor arrived at a quarter-past seven, accompanied by the Town Clerk, Alderman Hutchinson, Councillors Rogers and Peacock, Mr Elijah Place (market inspector), Mr Turner (superintenient of the Fire Brigade), and others "God save the Queen" having been played, The MAYOR, who stood on the stand among the re— volving "horses," said he Was present on behalf of the committee who had been appointed to prepare a suit- able reception for the W.rrington Volunteers when they returned, and to thank Mr. Wallis and Mr. Clarke for their generosity. They sent a large number of tni.n away at the beginning of the year to fight the battles of the Queen and country in South Africa. They honoured the men for the sacrifice they madeond th,45- promised them when they went away that on their return they would give them the hearty welcome they would richly de- serve. He Was glad those before him were rqually de- termined to show what they thought about such brave men. (Cheers.) He sincerely hoped that when the men returned Warringtna would keep up its reputation for good conduct, and that they would not have the town disgraced and discredited by scenes similar to those which took place in London on the return of the City Volunteers a few days ago. (Cheers.) He WAS very proud of Warrington and of the Warringtnn prople, and he helieve4 there WAS no town in Eneland—certainly not in Lancashire—where crowds behaved more creditably and fairly than they did in the good old town of Warrington. Therefore he wantod the people—especially the younger people, who might be inclined to become a little excited—'m nalke up their minds to do nothing calculated to injure the fair fame of the town of which they were so mond. (Cheers).— On the motion of Alderman Hutchinson cheers were given for the Mayor and Means. Wallis and Clarke.

div.head: HARRIERS.
div.p: HARRIERS.
Runcorn.

Runcorn Harriers journeyed to St Helens on Saturday to fulfil their inter-club run with Sacred Hearts.Runcorn were without the servivs of W Lewis and J Mathews while Sacred Hearts lacked the services of Mclntyre, This being the first meeting of the season great interest was taken in the race. Trail was laid over 71 miles of excellent counlry, including splendid jumps over both hedge and ditch. The weather was exce.dingly favour- able for cross-country sport, and brought out a good number of runners, there being 40 of the home team and a dozen of Runcorn making up the pack. Hopkins and Caldwell took the pace from the start, closely fol- lowed by lone, of Runcorn. It was a good race through- out and on the numbers being counted it was found that Runcorn ran out easy winners by 23 pouts. The follow- ing is the position of the teams.—Runcorn ; 3, Ince ; 4 Hopkins; 5, Goodall; 6, Stu hbs; 7, Leyland; 8, J Bignall total, 33 points. Sacred Hearts.-1. Cord well ; 2, J Whittle; 11, J Glynn; 13, Turno r; 14, Dare ; 15, Con naughton ; total, 56 points.

Good Templary. In celebration of the Jubilee of the Good Templar Order a covenant service was held at the Temperance Hall, Latchford on Mon- day evening. The chair was taken by Miss Hamp- ton, the lodge chief templar, who introduced the novenant service. The monthly meeting of the No 1 Convention, South-West Lancashire was held on Saturday,at Stubshaw Cross Ashton-in- Makerfield. Bro G Clarke, C.C.T. (Earlestown), pre- sided over a good attendance. The first business was the appointment of committees for credential and reporting purposes. After this had been accom- pliched, the C.C.T. presented his monthly report showing that the lodges in the area were doing good work, and urging all the members to make this year, which is the jubilee year of the Geod Templar Order, a success. Bro Brookes, C.E.S. (Leigh), reported on the electoral work, and in re- ferring to the recent General Election, said that the temperance question was more hopeful at the present time than it has been for some time past. The work among the juveniles was reported upon by Sister Mrs Woods, C.S.J.T. (Earlestewn), who stated that the juvenile branch was in a flourishing condition, an increase in membership being shown in the quarterly returns. The reports were adopted The report of Bro E Newman, C. Sec (Earlestown), showed a slight decrease in membership on the quarter,but there was a promise of good and useful work during the winter months. Bro A Lea (Liver- pool), then delivered an address on the work of the Order in general. It was decided to hold the next meeting at Warringtnn. After tea a public meeting was held, when Bre G Clarke, C.C,T , presided, and addresses were delivered by the Chairman and Bro A Lee (I,iverpoel). avid songs, reeitations. div.head: EXAMINER NRIDAY, NOVEMBER 23 1900.
div.p: THE EXAMINER NRIDAY, NOVEMBER 23 1900.

EARLESTOWN & NEWTON --- POLICE CASE. At the Police Court, Newton,on Tuesday morning before Mr. 1' J Gillespie, Thomas Trueman. a moulder, of Earlestown was charged with being drunk in Earlestown on Monday and was fined 2s 6d and costs. BAPTIST CHAPEL ANNIVERSARY. The anniversary services in connection with the Earlestown Baptist Church, was held on Sunday. The services were conducted by the Rev. J S Hughes of Hill Cliffa,Warrington,who also delivered impressive discourses from the pulpit. Special anthems and hymns were sung by the choir. P SA. The usual weekly meeting of the Earlestown District Society of the P S.A. was held in the C-- operative Hall,Earlestown on Sunday afternoon. Mr J J Leatherbarrow presided over a good attendance. Mr James Cryer of the Manchester City Mission gave an earnest address on "Faith, Hope and Love," Vocal items were given by Miss Tombs, and Mims Thomas presided at the piano. The collections were in aid of the Manchester City Mission.

SUDDEN DEATH AT NEWTON. On Monday afternoon a very sudden death took place at Newton. Henry Thomas Kitchen, 41 year-. of age, employed as a ruler at Messrs McCorquo dale and Uo'.9, printing works, and residing at Golbirne- road, Newton, had been suffering from a slight c 31,1 a week or two back. On Sunday last he went to visit 80M9 friends at Golborne, and when returning home he was seized with pains in the chest, his left side and arm. He went to work as usual on Mon- day morning and worked until noon. After dinner be was again seized with the pains. A neighbour applied flannels with turpentine and Dr. Watkins was sent for, but the man suddenly expired before medical aid arrived. Dr. Watkins put down the cause to a fainting fit. The coroner has been noti- fied of the death. GOOD TEMPLARY. The Hope of Earlestown Lodge meeting was held in Wargrave Hall on Monday evening, Bro Cutler, C.T., presiding. After the opening services the programme committee presented their report which recommended a jubilee covenant service, it being the jubilee of the Order which was founded at Ithaca, New York, fifty years ago. Bro Newman gave the report of No I Cmvention, and the greet- ings of the "Offspring of Hope" Lodge, Tyldesley.— The programme being a musical evening and coffee supper it was opened by the singing of the ode " Hark the temperance bells."—Piano solo, Bro Willis; song, " I'm Hiding," Sister Newman ; recita- tion, "The Station Master's Story," Bro Warburton; song, "Genevieve." Bro T Macklin , recitation, " What the train brought," Bro Roberts, of Cafn ; pianoforte duet, "Whisperings of Love," Sister Miss Woods! and Miss Dickens; reading, Bro Woods; pianoforte duet, "Fairy Wedding Waltz," Sister Miss Woods and Miss Dickens, encored.—Bro Clarke pro- posed and Bro Warburton seconded a vote of thanks to those taking partvand to the committee (Sister S. Woods and Sister Ord), who provided the refresh- ments which were served at the close of the lodge.

EARLESTOWN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY. - The 160th quarterly meeting of this Society, was held in the Cc-operative Hall, Earlestown, on Mon- day evening. There was a fair attendance of mem- bers and Mr D Forrester presided. The report and balance sheet showed the 'cash receipts to be £9,648 64 1111 being an increase over last quarter of £69 12s 40, and of £560 9s 31-over the corres- ponding period last year. The nett profits realised were £1,476 17s sid, which were disposed of by pav- ing a dividend of 3s in the .£ requiring £1,455 16s 6d,; £lO to a new reserve fund to be terme Workmen's Compensation Fund; and the balance I.£ll Os 110 to Dividend Reserve Fund. During the quarter 47 new members had • been admitted and 31 had withdrawn,leaving 1,589 on the register, of whom 1,196 had brought in checks. The balance sheet was adopted. Messrs J G Mullins and Peter Parr were re-appointed on the Committee of Management without opposition. Mr D Forre,iter was nominated for the position of president. Mr W Gilmour submitted hie report as delegate to the Co-operative wholesale meeting. A grant of £5 was voted from the patter's profits towards the Viaduct Institute Technical Instruction prize fund. It was stated that classes had been instituted for instruction to the young in ce-operative principles, and in support of the project a sum of £5 was voted. It was intimated that the plans which were submit- ted for the proposed stabling, cart-shed, cottage and dairy, had been passed by the Council, and after some discussion the committee were authorised to proceed with the work, the estimated cost being £B5O. Owing to the unsuitability of the premises now occupied by the Society in Upper Earle-street as a branch shop, and to the fact that the lease would expire within the next 12 months, it was proposed to build a new shop in accordance with the plans produced, which also included a cottage The proposal of the Committee was approved by the meeting. Authority was also given for the building of cottages for the members in accordance with the rules of the Society. MANCHESTER CITY MISSION, EARLESTOwN BRANCH. "-7. A. meeting in connection with the above was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, on Tuesday evening, when an address on the work of the Mis- sion ',vas given by Mr. J. Cryer, of Manchester.—Mr O Dring, the local Missionary, submitted a report of the Mission, in which it was stated that the Man- chester City Mission had a staff of 82 agents, 47 missionaries, and 24 deaconeaaes, wholly employed, and 11 part time workers. In 1899 its agents paid ' 260,767 visits to the homes of the people for the purpose of reading the Scripture, religious conver- sation and prayer. The workhouses, lodging-houses, infirmaries, night asylums, fever and small-pox noi- pitals. 80., were also amongst the list of places specially vi.ited, one Missionary having, during his life's work, paid not less than 5,000 visits to small- pox patients. In 22 Mission Halle, as centres of religious energy and enterprise, there were held Gospel services, Ragged Schools, Bands of Hope, and Bible Classes. and in connection therewith, open-air services, cottage meetings, mothers' meet- ing., &a, From the people associated with the Mission Halls, upwards of £2,000 was raised in one year for the maintenance of the work at the various halls where it was collected, and acknowledged in their local reports, Roughly speaking, there were annual subscribers who steadily provided some £5OO vet annum to enable the Board of the City Mission to carry on its work, but beyond this, some £2,500 was needed for which the Board was dependent on , legacies, special donations and special collections. For well nigh a quarter of a century Earlestown had been supplied with the Missionary. through a continuous subscription to the City Mission by Mrs Evans, for that purpose. In 1886 the Earlestown District Association was formed in order to give opportunity far the friends out here to show practi- cal sympathy by contributing to the work in the Cit-. During these years Earlestown had raised £l7O as a direct contribution to aid the City Mission in its work in Manchester. In 1899 the Earlestown contribution was £5 7s 2d. THE PROPOSED NEW PUBLIC CLOCK AT NEWToN. On Wednesday evening a meeting of parishioners was held in the vestry of St. Peter's Church, New- ton, for the purpose of giving the wardens the necessary statutory authority to apply to the Ecclesiastical Commissioners for a faculty to enable them to place in the new tower, which is approach- ing completion, a clock and chimes, and a peal of eight bells. The Rev J H Ryder presided and amongst Others present were—Messrs J Liptrott (warden', J Simpson, T Mayer, 0 Clarke, R Barton and Pereival.—The Chairman read the notice con- vening the meeting, and said the business we, the first nitre to obtain a faculty to permit the Urban District Connell to place a clock in the tower of the church. The Council imposed a con- dition that the clock when it, was placed in the church,should be theproperty of the District Coun- cil, and thus the property of the people generally. The clock at present as far as they knew, was to have three or four faces, and it was to be illumin- ated and kept in repair by the District Council. Hs wanted the vestry to anthorise himself and the churchwardens to apply for a faculty to put the clock in the tower of the church, and when the faculty was applied for it, would be heard before the Chancellor of the thocese,and if he thought it a fit and proper thing to do,he would accede to the re- quest of that, meeting and grant a faculty. Included in the application wasipermision to hang a peal of eight bells. He did not mean to say that they had actually got the bells' but he hoped it would not he long before they did get tliem, still it was neces- sary for them to obtain a faculty for the purpose. Mr R Barton proposed that the wardens and Vicar have authority to apply for the faculty in accor- dance with the particulars given by the Chairman. Mr John Simpson seconded. Mr Clarke asked sup- posing a peal of bells was not put in the tower, and they wanted chimes for the clock, did the faculty cover the chime. ? Mr Barton said he thought the faculty for a clock would include the chimes. The motion was then put and unanimously carried'

Apart from other considerations, this is an injustice to the publican, who may see boats going past his house, fitted with open bars and doing a roaring trade during hours when his own premises must be closed by law. So in theatres a dramatic license, whether granted by Royal Patent, or by county council, or by the ius- tices, carries with i a right to excise liquor licenses and it is a doubtful point how far, if at all, closing regulations apply. In all these cases, the sale of liquor should be subjected to the control of the licensing authority; at present in Ireland a justices' license is already required for the wholesale beer- dealer's license.

There are of course many other points in which the law might be improved. Its present complexity is a great bar to its proper administration both by the licensing authority and the police. Ignorance of the law often tends to throw the justices more and more upon their clerks, for guidance and advice. The clerk is not disqualified from acting as they are themselves by holding brewery shares, and sometimes does business for brewers on his own account as a solicir, or, sometimes even appearing on behalf of brewers before neighbouring benches, so that it may be difficult for him to approach the consideration of a matter in which his client is interes ed, with perfect freedom from bias. With- out throwing any discredit on the general body of justices' clerks, who discharge with honesty and credit their multifarious and responsible duties, it would be well for them to be disqualified from act- ing in licensing matters on the same principle as the justices themselves. Other changes in the law are made necessary by defects in the licensing authority itself, which we will now proceed to consider.

DEFECTS IN THE LICENSING AUTHORITY. We have seen that a good deal of the present ex- cess of licensed houses is due to ill-considered legis- lation, hut most of the failure of licensing adminis- tration is due to defects on the part of the licensing authority. There is a slight difference in the organisation of the licensing authority in boroughs and county districts, though in both it consists solely of the justices of the peace. In boroughs applications for new licenses are dealt with by a licensing com— mittee of justices, and if granted have to be con- firmed by the full bench. Applications for renewals of old licenses are dealt with by the full bench, an appeal against the refusal of a renewal on a trans- fer goes, not to the quarter sessions of the borough itself, if it has.any, but to thejustices of the county in which it is situated, assembled at quarter ses- sions, in which the borough justices have no lot or part. In counties applications for new licenses or renewals are dealt with by the full benlh of the petty sessional division, but new grants have to be confirmed by the County Licensing Committee, elected by the Justices at quarter sessions, and appeals against refusal of renewal or transfer are heard by the justices at county quarter sessions. WlThus the county justices are in a peculiarly re- sponsible position, for they not only sit as licensing authority in the first instance,but they-hear appeals from boroughs, however large, even from county boroughs, as well as from the county itself. We shall return later to an examination of their con- duct on the hearing of appeals The deficiencies of the licensing justices in the first instance have been chiefly sins of.omission. They found an unsatisfactory Kate of things, due partly to defective law, and partly to the neglect of their predecessors in office, and while they have not often done enything positive to make it worse, they have still more seldom done anything to make it better. Their rule has been that of a Bing Log. After a close and careful examination of all Ms.., facts it cannot be denied that their administration has been a slack one, and unfortunately slackness is not a quality to be commended espec'ally when the forces tending to the extension of the liquor traffic are not slack, but on the contrary almost abnormally active, and backed by the enormous power of capital. This of course is a general statement.. There are many individual justices, and some whole benches whose activity, and energy, and wisdom, ia the per- formance of their difficult duties cannot be too highly praised, who have devoted much time and thought to the study of the problems presented to them. But these are unfortunately the exceptions, and by shewing how much can be done, tbey very often illustrate the more clearly how much has been left undone by thsir neighbours.. The adminis- tration of the Justices of Itngland and Wales may be said to stand midway in point of efficiency between that of the not perfect but still better administration of the justices an i magistrates in Scotland, and the altogether worthless,if not almost 'corrupt, maladministration of the justices in Ire- land. It must also be allowed that the English justices of to-lay are much better than they were and more alive to their responsibilities. Few jus- tices are now to be found like the chairman of a bench of justices in Wales, who made it his boast that he had never refused any application for a license, not from any theory about the benefits of free licensing but apparently oat of mere natural stupidity and perverseness. In our next article we sball proceed to consider the administration of the licensing justices more in detail.

div.head: iii. Causes of the Failure of Licensing Administration.
div.p: iii. Causes of the Failure of Licensing Administration.

For 400 years the administration of the licensing laws has been in the hands of the justices, and the result is, as we have seen, that. the face of the country is covered with an inordinate number of licensed house, while the evils arising from this excess are aggravated by the tied house system; in spite of the careful selection supposed to be made in choosing "fit and proper" persons to hold licen- ses, publicans as a class cannot be said to be in any degree superior to their unselected neighbours. Such a result can only be described as a failure; an examination of its cAuses shows that two things have contributed, defects in the law, and defects in the licensing authority.

div.head: DRFECTS TN ,THE LAW.
div.p: DRFECTS TN ,THE LAW.

It is impossible for the. liWnsi;g.. authority to properly administer the law, unless they have an irresistible weapon in their hands, by which to enforce the execution of their wishes. It is impos- sible to lay down exactly in an Act of Parliament the numberless details over which the licensing authority must exercise control, it is not only impos- sible, but also undesirable. The size of the licensed premises, their construction as to internal arrange- ments, bar, sitting accommodation, back doors, side door and so on, special conditions as to their use and many other particulars are matters which are exceedingly important in themselves, but the con- trol of the licensing authority is better secured by giving them absolute discretion to refuse the license altogether than by specifying their particular powers in a list, in which any points not mentioned would be held to be definitely excluded To con- trol the tied-house system the licensing authority must be able to say "Unless the conditions of the tenancy are such as we can approve, we will not grant the license at all." Now the justices do possess this absolute discretionary power of refusal in case of all fully licensed house, and in fact of all on-licensed houses except those beer and wine houses which have been licensed continuously since before May, 1869 (commonly known as the ante- -1869 beer houses), and in some places they have used their power to obtain improvements in the structural conditions,Bcc , and even to prevent chil- dren under age being served,with very good results. The ante-1869 beer houses stand on a different footing and it will be well to give some account of these houses and their origin ; for their history is very instructive, and illustrative of the mistakes which may be made by well meaning people. Up till 1830 there was only one kind of house licensed for consumption on the premises, namely the alehouse, or fully licensed house, where all kinds of liquors were sold ; these were under the complete discretion of the justices, who were even in some few cases accused of exercising their power arbitrarily. In 1830 an Act was passed practically enabling anyone who wished, to start a beerhouse on payment of a small fee ; the object of the promo- ters of the Act was twofold, partly to break down the tied house system', and partly to discourage the consumption of spirits, which was then ve,y large, by encouraging the consumption of the less alcoholic beer. Never did the intentions of well- meaning people meet with more disastrous failure now beer houses, it is true, sprang immediately in- o existence, but drunkenness increased enor- mously. and while the consumption of beer crew by leaps and bounds, the consumption of spiri.s was only stimulatedln )1. did the tied-house system cease to flourish The effect on the administra- tion of the licensing law was also very bad: It was useless for the justices to abolish a fully licensed house, if its place could be immediately taken by two beer houses, and sometimes they even granted the full spirit license td a beer house in order to get it under some kind of control.Comrcritt ee after commit- tee of Lords and Commons reported most strongly against the beer houses. According to Mr. Villiers's Committee in 1854,they fermed amischievous refuge for those who had failed disreputably or been deprived of their licenses as publicans. They were the "habitual haunts of idle- and abandoned, of thieves, prostitutes, and the adepts and teachers of crime

div.head: " ON " ANTE-1869 BEEILHOUSES
div.p: THE " ON " ANTE-1869 BEEILHOUSES

At last, in 1869, a change was made all new beerhouses for consumption both on or off had to *obtain a certificate from the justices refusable at discretion; beerhouses then existing had also to obtain a Justices certificate, aut this was oily re- fusable on one of four grounds, viz., character of the applicant, disorderly conduct of the house, dis- qualification of applicant by forfeiture of a previ- ous license or misconduct, rack of qualification in the applicant or the house. i.e. the house being under a certain annual rating, or the applicant not b,ing, the resident occupier. Practically the license can only be refused on account of the bad character of the applicant, or the disorderly con- duct of the house.

The off beerhouses were made subject to the full discretion of the justices in 1880-2, and a great number of them were refused in consequence. But in spite of this precedent the "on " ante-1869 beer- houses still retain the same position, privileged in comparison with the fully licensed houses, though of course reduced below their original status. The four grounds of refusal fall far short of the free and unlimited discretion which we have pointed out as essential to. proper administration by the licensing authority. The privileged beerhouses, though reduced to about 30,000 in number from about 50,000 in 1869, stand like a block in the way of any reform, especially in some of the great towns, e q., Manchester and Birmingham. In Birmingham hundreds of them are so placed as to render proper supervision impossible, many having back doors leading into common yards The justices cannot press reforms, e.g.., non-serving of children, find their wishes disregarded, and an effec- tual obstacle presented to suggested improvements. In Manchester the result of the law is said to be "to perpetuate in excessive numbers dirty, ill-con- structed, and unsuitable licensed premises, which no bench of justices at the present day would tolerate."

The same story comes from many other places, and it is worth remarking thv the tenant of an ante-1869 beerhouse may be worse off than o'hers, because he may find his license transferred to an- o her at the will of the brewer, the absence of the consent of the transferor not being one of the s'atutory grounds of refusual. There can be no doubt that the privileged be4rhouses have done harm enough already in the 30 years during which they have enjoyed their superior position, and they ought at once to be placed on the same footing as other licensed houses.

The discretion of the licensing authority is limited in a similar manner in regard to a certain class of off licenses, namely those under which spirits and wine are sold in bo'tles : in some cases indeed of retail off licenses, no justices' license at all is re- quired. These spirit and wine licenses form part of what are popularly known as grocer's licenses, to which we shall return at a later stage. but the only point at present is their immunity from the free and unqualified discretion to which even off beer licenses have been subjected since 1892. So anoma— lous is the law that, while the justices can refuse a license to sell a bottle of beer, they practically can- not refuse a license to sell a bottle of brandy. The difference only needs stating to make it clear that a uniformity of law with regard to all classes of licenses is most desirable.

There are a few minor cracks in the law, which need to be stopped. deserving of mention. Whole- sale licenses are taken out directly from the excise on payment of a certain sum, and do not require a justices' certificate at all These, and especially the wholesale beer license allowing the sale of beer in gallon casks, are frequently made the cover for illicit sales by retail, which are 'very difficult to prove. Anyone may hold this license even in the face of repeated convictions. One man in Cardiff, for instance,was convicted five times of shebeening or illicit sale in one house, and altogether 15 times in 10 years. yet he was still able to take out the license The evil has been especially notic Aable in the case of large bodies of workmen collected to- gether for the construction of railway works, or waterworks; a specially flagrant case occurred in the making of the Manchester Ship Canal. The mischief is aggravated by the fact that the sale under those licenses is not subject to the ordinary restriction of hours either on Sundays or week days-

Again no justices' license is required for the sale of intoxicants on hoard passenger boats.going from one port of the United Kingdom to another or returning to the same port on the same day. This exemption covers passenger boats plying on rivers. In the port of London, however, no sale is allowed on vessels at anchor during the ordinary closing hours, and in Scotland no sale is allowed on:Sun- days. Fearful scenes of drunkenness have been

div.head: (coNTiNtTED.). NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN•
div.p: (coNTiNtTED.). NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN•
[BY A CORSESPON'DENT.I

The Earlestown Co-operative Society judging by its last quarterly report is making rapid strides in the marcn of prog:ess. For some tiine past it has steadily paid a dividend of three shillings in the .2, and its sales have almost reached five figures for the quarter. They have now taken in bawl the task of spending some of their money in n-w buildings, but the undertaking which will givs most satisfac- tion is the erection of cottages to be billoted for by the members. The scarcity of houses in Earlestown is a well known and inconvenient fact, but the pro- posal of the Co-operative Society will go some way to relieve the pressure, although it will not be ad- vantageous to landlords.

Lord Newton's agent still defiei the District Council in respect of the slice of Common land wnich he has appropriated and enclosed. Certainly the land is not much, but it is sufficient to put the ratepayers and their representatives on their met. tie. Why on earth ws cannot have a strong rate- payers' Association in Earlestown, I cannot under- stand, because such an Association would be of im- mense help to the Council in such matters as these. To some extent this species of land-grabbing would be checked because a small annual contribution to the Common Rights Protection. Association would bring to their side a very powerful factor in oppos- ing such encroachments.

As it has now been definitely decided to open up almost immediately, the new street leading fram Wargrave-road to Crow-lane, it is to be hoped those who have the letting of the land for building pur- poses will take especial care to see that only houses of a good class are erected. We are without a good residential neighbourhood, and there is an excellent opportunity in the opening of the road in question to eff )r,l facilities for the erection of good houses or villas of a class rather above the ordinary cot- tage.

Brick-street Independent Methodist Band of Hope. The 2nd entertainment was given in the Mission Hall, on Tuesday evening under the presidency of Mr. James Shaw. There was a very good attendance The chairman gave the children some practical advice, and pointed out that the object of Band of Hope meetings was to instil into their minds tem- perance principles, so that they may grow up sober men and women. An interesting programme was provided, which gave much pleasure. The follow- ing recited : Carry Taylor, Ethel Bibby, Polly Highara, Emily Howard, Emily Holmes, James Barton, John Howell, James Wilson, and Thomas Gallop. The Band of Hope Choir gave two choruses viz., "Men for the Times," and "Glorious News." Miss Cissy Holt rendered successfully the solos "Someone's Child," and" Tapping on the Window Pane" Two violin solos entitled "The song that reached my heart," and "Scenes that are brightest" ware given by Master Stanley Tomkinson, and the following dialogues "The New Banner" " Why Father Christmas doant come," and " Wanted a Cook" proved very instructive and enjoyable. The singing of the Doxology brought to a close a profit- able evening.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.

[By " OvaUsti Why cannot a team which thrashes Rochdale Hornets by 21 pointslone week, safely account for Barrow, the following week? By all the considerations which govern football calculations Warrington should have had a fairly easy journey with the Barrovians, who had only one win to their credit, yet the opposite happened. The question asked at the beginning of the paragraph is practically implssible to answer where a team like War- rington is concerned. Truly they are the most incon- sistent lot in. Lancashire-3 reputation which Widnes once held. 'ri9 mere repetition to talk about dis- appointment and disgrace. The Warrington team prr,- vides both with such frequency as to become almost monetonoua. Still it does make one a bit disgusted with football when the fifteen one remllarly supperts cmes and gets wiped out in such summary and unex- pected fashion:

Fancy ailowing Barrow, the new converts from the second division, to rub in 14 points to five—almost double the score any team has so far been able to record against Warrington. And not only that, but the visitors escaped very well with strth a result. It might very easily have been ten points more. ghe winners were a long way the best team and made things exceed- ingly warm the whole of the time play was in progress. ll the scoring was the outcome of excellent, even superior combination and science on their part. There were no scrambling forward rushes and flaky tries. No! the ball was whipped out and handled by man after man in just the fashion that won Warrington thn Previous game. There was no hesitation about the Barrow men and their dash and energy should get them many more points than they possess at pressnt.

RN The ground was on the heavy side, and thin militated againsc Warrington's chances against the heavier men opp)sed to them,but this is the only excuse it is possible to scrape up. Warrington's wedkness was strikingly emphasised and it is a pity that the whole of the commit- teo did not have the opportunity of seeing their chosen fifteen so handsomely Wren down. The expected hap- pened in one respect, for Warrington wer hopelessly beaten in the forward division. Treweeke and Co easily held the upper hand and heeled out when they liked without putting anything like their maximum strength into the lob. Four new men of 13 stone odd—all 1)3 in and muscle—would jut about make up Warrington'i deficiency in this dep Lament.

On man alone did himself justice on the Warrington side and, of course, it was Fish. He played an astound- ing game and in addition to scarin,g W;irrinE:ton's five points, he saved his side repeatedlY. The Barrow men were wonderfully impressed with his abilities, and the way he dodged through them time after time was some- thing entirely new in their eyes. The Barrow critic is quite right when he says that Fish stood head and shoulders above the rest, and he is not far wrong when he adds that there was only one threequarter on the Warrington side and that was Fish. On the defence he was not backed up as he shnul I have been, and when Barrow scored the last try the iittle wing man was left with three men to tackle. Warrington's centres were again weak, and there w,il have to b 3 a change here before the table of roses changes satisfactorily. Bur- gess and Duckworth are deserving of some praise for the way they stuck ta their work under difficulties. The former sustained painful injury whieh prevented him being at his best:for the remainder of the game.
The Lancashire League table up to date stands as follows :

The position of the leaders has not altered since our last issue, Swinton once more winning their match. Runcorn made mincemeat of Wigan, who were walloped by 34 points to five on the Runcorn ground. This is a performance which stamps the " Linnets" as beiog in their best form once more. Oldham had an easy journty against Widnes, while the Rangers lowered the number of the Leigh men at Broughton. Millom ran the Hor- nets to a goal at Rochdale and must be counted un- lucky to have got so near and yet failed.

Warrington are playing away again this week. St. Helens being the opponents today. The teams have met once this season at Warrington, when there was no soars so that the advantage apoears to rest with the Saints. They however, were badly beaten by Salford last Saturday on their own ground, and there are more impossible things than that Warrington might repeat their performance in their cup-tie last season. I don't expect them to do so, but I shall be pleased to congratu— late them if they do.

A few changes have been made in the team which lost at Barrow. Holkenhall is replaced by Harris, who certainly did not earn his place by his play in the "A".tearn match last week. Neither did Taylor,. but he is promoted to the first team again, M'ereweather and Andrews are also included in the forwards, the retiring scrummagers being Antrobus, Jolley-and Swift, jun. Could the poverty of the club for capable players be more anparent than in this juggling about of medio- crities?

By the way Leigh have been fortunate enough to PAcure W Pearson the Swinton half-back who couid not find a place in the Blues' premier team. Last season he was contain of the "Lions," and he has been !Alvin& vary well for the second team of late. A couple of months ago I suggested to a Warrington club official that an effort should be made to secure Pearson,but the idea was pooh-poohed. Price too high, etc.—Swinton won't part and so on. Leigh have got him,however, and they are a noorer club by a lot than Warrington. It is no use the Warrington Club making the excuse that good men cannot be got. The fact is there—other clubs keep getting them.

div.head: FIRE AT EATRLESTOWN.
div.p: FIRE AT EATRLESTOWN.

On Friday night a fire broke out on the premises of Mr. E T Evans, Market-street. Earlestown, draper and clothier. All the employ& bad left the place, and the establishment was locked up about 10.15. About 10.30 a young fellow named James Moly- neux going home by the back street behind Mr Evans' premises, noticed fire in what prayed to be the tailor's workroom, end which is close to the room where the firewood is kept. Molyneux ran to inform some of Mr Evans' employ6s, but an assistant employed at Mr Littler's, named George Chandley, overhearing Molyneux giving the alarm, ran to the back door and burst it open. He got a bucket, and with water endeavoured to check the flames. In the meantime other people came on the scene and rendered esqistance, and the police obtained the fire hose from the Town Hall and there being a good supply of water the fire was speedily extinguished before it had got a firm hold It is estimated that £l2 worth of damage has been done chiefly by the water. How the fire originated is at pre4ent a mystery.

THE EXAMINER FRI I )NY NOVEMBER, 23, 190 C EMMANUEL CHURCH. The Annual Sale of Work. Opening- oy Mr. Cicero Smith. During the past few days the members of the coueregation of Emmanuel Church, have been making strenuous efforts by means of a sale of work to augment the funds for the maintenance of the church services, Sunday Schools, Christian -Endeavour Societies, and other agencies in the parish. It is stated that this year there has been a tailing off in the income owing to removals and other causes. A debt also remains on the church building, which it is desired to remove before the close of the year. The sale was opened last Wednes- day afternoon, in the schoolroom over Arpley- Station. The stalls had been 'very effectively erranged,being draped with muslin of various tints, and fair ladies did their utmost to induce visitors to purchase the many articles so temptingly dis- played. Below is a list of the stalls and stallisolders : —Mrs Reed's stall,Mrs E T Reed,Mrs G Norman,aliss A B Monk ; cougreaational stall, Mrs William Atherton, Mrs Armstrong, Mrs Smith, Mr William Atherton ; Christian Endeavour stall, Miss Lees, Miss Eva Lees, Mies Mason, Miss Jenks, Mr W Dickens, Mr J Hodge, Misses Lettie and Annie Ashbrook, and Miss E Taylor; flower and fruit stall : Mrs Smithson, Miss A. Harding, Miss Elsie Taylor, Miss Matilda Moores, Mr James Callon ; Sunday sctiool stall, Mrs A Gandy, Miss Lloyd, Mrs Habert Landon, Mrs. John Lloyd, Miss Mivards, Mrs Frank Lloyd ; children's stall : Miss Ethel Hodge, Miss Nellie Matthews, and Miss Dorrie Gibbons ; refreshment stall and tea room : Mrs Henry Gandy, Miss Allen, Mrs alinards, Mrs flallwood, Mrs H Yule, Mrs Eccles, Mrs Miles, Mrs Matthews, and Miss Annetta Mee. There was a good attendance at the opening ceremony amongst those present being the Rev E T Reed (vicar), and Mrs Reed, Mr Cicero Smith, of Soutbport, (who opened the sale), Mrs Smith, the Revs John Yonge, T Bishop and JF Matthews. After a hymn had beea sung, and prayer offered by the Rev T;Bishop, The Rev E T REED, who presided, said that as it was desirable that the opening proceedings should not be unduly prolonged it would save time if certain letters which had been received were read at once. The presi- ding Bisaop of the Cnurcla (Bishop Eldridge) wrote as follows:—"I sincerely trust that your Sale of Work will be a great success, greater even than any you have had. We shall pray for you, that the Lsrl may give his bier- siug on your united efforts, and dispose the hearts of his people to much liberality on your behalf. May you have health and streagth for the arduaus work, and ob- tain an abundant reward. Kindly convey the expres- sion of my Christian love and good wishes to all your people, and especially to the dear young friends of the Christian Eadeavour Society." Miss Bessie Dutton, whose kindness had been shown on many former occa- sions, wrote :—"Dear Mrs Reed,l am making a little visit to my brother here and shall not be at home before your sale takes place. lam sorry, for I have always enjoyed coming and I do trust it will be a great success and as pleasant as ever." Mr. Cuncillor J G Graves of Shef- field also wrote and increased his subscription. Mr. Reed proceeded to read a list of donations and collections which totalled to £3O 15s 6i. In introducing Mr. Cicero Smith, who was he said, au old friend of his wife's, and a more re- cent though none the lesa real friend of his own, he felt particularly grateful to him for so readily coming to open the sale en this occasion ; for the past year had been one of special difficulty and trial, more so indeed than any year of his ministry in Warrington. This was moreover, the third time in nine years that Mr Smith had opened their sale and they had 01:00 ed- ingly pleasant receneetiane of the genial and en couraging way in which he went abaat a mongst them on the two previous occasions. T his year the sale had been brought to its present state by fewer workers than usual ; but he should like to say how mucta he personally appreciated the faithful and constant service of those who had stood by the work during a difficult year. Their devotion was worshv of all comrneadation and they would find their reward in the successful work which he had no doubt would be done by their churn in the future. Their sincere and cordial thanks were also tendered to all the friends, far and near, wh ) had so kindly helped them on tnis occa- sion by donations of money or goods. By their practical sympathy they had placed them under great obligations which they would try to repay by increased devotion to the work of the Master. A little over an hour ago he received a telegram to the effect that not only was Mr. Smith comiug, but that he was to be accompanied by his excellent wife whom they were delighted to see that afternom (Applause.) After some humorous opening observations Mr CICERO SALIM said ho had felt for many years that the main difficulty in religious matters was that there was a tendency on the part of many people towards an elabor- ate external kind of service, or ritualism, and on the other hand taare was a vast amount of indifference. He did not know whether they had studied the question very carefully, but after consideration he had Come to the conclusion that both conditions arose from one thing, and that was the realization in the Christian church of the spirit of service. rho main principle that Jesus Christ laid down was " I am among you as one to serve. Be that will he cbief among you, let him be your servant." The congregations, he was afraid, particularly among their Nonconformist brethren, wanted to be served too much and not serve quite enough. They were sometimes rather too:hard upon the ministers, and expected a little bit too much from them. They at Emmanuel Church had made a protest against the ritualism of the Church of England according to their consciences, by separating themselves from it to a large extent, and from what he knew of Mr- and Mrs Reed, he was sure that whatever work they en gaged in, was some faithful, honest and loyal work for Christ. In conclusion he wished the sale every success and hoped the workers would be able to look back with satisfaction and joy upon the three days they were going to spend at this blessed work. (Applause.) Mr REED mentioned that at their last annual sale of work they had the presence of the Mayor and Mayoress of Warrington, and they were glad that Alderman and Mrs Roberts bad been re-elected to that honourable position. (Applause.) They had not their presence upon that occasion because the calls upon them were so numerous that be (Mr Reed) thought it would have seemed very inconsiderate to have asked them to come again. However,they had with them the Mayor's chap- lain, the Rev John Yonge, who had proved a good friend to him (the speaker) ever since he came to Warrington. lie would ask him to propose a hearty vote of thanks to Mr and Mrs Smith for their kindness ia atteadiag the sale. In mo eaag tte vote of thanks, the Rev. John Yonge said he wss sure that by coming there that day, Mr and Mrs Smite had rendered a very valuable service to Mr Reel anti nis people. Those of them who had the plea- sure of fis quently meeting Mr and Mrs Reed and mem- bers of the congregation knew how earnestly and de- votedly they were all endeavouring to carry on the cause to which they had given themselves. They had felt a depression cf circumstances, as all congregations had felt, but they were living in the hope that as the new century dawned and as it proceeded, they were going to see brighter conditions in things temporal and 'spiritual. (Applause). Mr PAGE seconded the motion which was carried with acclamation. Mr Smart briefly acknowledged the compliment, and the (mewing proceedings terminated with the singing of , the Doxolosty. The business of the day was then proceeded with. Thursday's Proceedings. The sale was re-opened on Thursday afternoon by Mr James Dodds, of Penketh, who was accompanied by his wife. The Rev E T Reed announced that the previous day's araceeds amounted to £B5 6i, and as that was an increase of £7 14s 83 upon the sum received on the first day of lase year's sale Ise thought they had much reason to he thankful for the result of Wednesday's proceedinge. He had to announce that he received a donation of £5 from Mr Samuel Smith. M.P. who had, on several occasions in the past, kindly helped them in this way. It was especially proper that this help should come frern him because of the commendable stand he had taken in Parliament on behalf of the Pro- testant and Evangelical truth and also an behalf of the public morals of the country. He bad also received a note from Sir George Williams, Bart, of London, enclos- ing a cheque for a guinea. His name was known all over the world as the founder of the Young Men's Christian Association. After alluding gratefully to several other donations, Mr Reed mentioned that Mr Dodds had just put into his hands a cheque for £5 for which they tendered him their hearty thanes (Applause.) Mr DODDS, in declaring the sale open, expressed his appreciation of the robust, manly and consistent character of their minister, the Rev E T Reed. That church was standing up manfully for the grand princi- ples which were established at the Reformation, but which of late, he was • afraid, had been endangered by a tendency in the Church of England to Romanisrn and Romish practices. When the people of the country understood these principles, 11
